Proposal for Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, C3 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.  
• Readouts  
  – Reduction in C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 deposition on RPE surface by immunofluorescence or ELISA (Holers, 2014).  
  – Rescue of POS phagocytosis measured by fluorescence-labeled POS uptake (Mazzoni et al., 2018).  
  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).  
• Mechanistic anchoring  
  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.  
  – Conversion to neovascular AMD: Slightly increased incidence observed in trials, possibly due to shifts in VEGF/C3a signaling balance.  
  – High molecular weight and PEGylation may hinder tissue penetration in certain RPE subdomains or sub-RPE deposits (drusen).  
  – Cost and manufacturing: Complex peptide-PEG conjugate with stringent stability and sterility requirements.  
  – Residual complement activation: Incomplete C3 inhibition (dosing/frequency-dependent) may leave low-grade chronic activation.  
Conclusion  
Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. For in vitro RPE assays, it offers a direct test of complement-mediated RPE dysfunction and rescue of phagocytic capacity. Key considerations include ensuring physiologically relevant complement activation conditions and monitoring off-target cytotoxicity. Given existing clinical data, progressing pegcetacoplan into refined RPE/POS co-culture assays should strongly inform potential biomarkers of efficacy and dosing strategies ahead of further in vivo or translational studies.

Proposal for Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura, C5 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. It was discovered by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) against human complement component 5 (C5) and subsequently optimized for high-affinity binding (Kd ~70 pM) and nuclease resistance. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures to bind specific protein targets; pegylated RNA aptamers have precedent in ophthalmology (e.g., pegaptanib for VEGF in wet AMD).

Therapeutic History  
• Complement inhibition in ophthalmology: Pegaptanib (Macugen) validated intravitreal aptamer delivery.  
• Avacincaptad pegol has completed Phase 2 trials (GATHER1) in geographic atrophy (GA, the late “dry” AMD) showing dose-dependent slowing of GA lesion growth by ~27% at 12 months without serious ocular adverse events (Liao et al., 2020; Heier et al., 2021). GATHER2 (Phase 3) is ongoing.  
• No prior veterinary uses. No reports of avacincaptad pegol outside GA. Other systemic C5 inhibitors (eculizumab) treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome but have not shown efficacy in AMD when dosed systemically, likely due to poor ocular penetration.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: Avacincaptad pegol binds the β-chain of C5, sterically preventing C5 convertase from cleaving C5 into C5a and C5b (Fielder et al., 2018).  
• Downstream effects:  
  – Inhibition of C5a generation abrogates C5a-mediated activation of C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1/CD88) on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and resident microglia, thus reducing NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Anderson et al., 2013; Doyle et al., 2012).  
  – Blockade of C5b prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9), reducing sublytic MAC deposition on RPE that otherwise disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity and impairs phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Kariko et al., 2013).  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express C5R1 (RNA-seq data, Kalliora et al., 2018) and are susceptible to complement-mediated inflammasome activation when exposed to drusen components or oxidized POS in vitro (Zhou et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Phagocytosis Assay  
In an in vitro assay in which human RPE cells are challenged with photo-oxidized POS or drusen-like material:  
• Complement activation normally drives C5a release, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (caspase-1 cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 secretion), and sublytic MAC deposition on RPE, elevating lysosomal pH and inhibiting cathepsin D–dependent POS degradation (Zhou et al., 2018; Kariko et al., 2013).  
• Addition of avacincaptad pegol to conditioned medium should neutralize nascent C5, abolishing C5a-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing MAC formation.  
• Predicted readouts:  
  – Reduced IL-1β and IL-18 in supernatant (ELISA).  
  – Lower levels of MAC deposition on RPE (immunofluorescence for C5b-9).  
  – Normalized lysosomal pH (LysoSensor assays) and cathepsin D activity.  
  – Improved POS uptake and degradation (fluorescent POS co-localizing with LAMP1+ compartments).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a terminal step in the complement cascade implicated by genetic (CFH, C3, C5 polymorphisms) and histopathological studies in dry AMD.  
• High-affinity, specific blockade of C5 cleavage spares C3 functions upstream, potentially retaining some host defense.  
• Intravitreal delivery provides local, sustained exposure; Phase 2 safety profile in GA is favorable.  
• Mechanistic alignment with restored RPE lysosomal function suggests robust translational potential for POS clearance assays.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Complement is only one contributor to dry AMD; oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction also play major roles. Monotherapy may only partially halt progression.  
• Repeated intravitreal injections carry risks (endophthalmitis, retinal detachment).  
• Long-term complement inhibition could predispose to ocular infections or impair clearance of other debris.  
• Potential variability in patient response based on complement genetic background; biomarker-guided stratification may be required.  
• Current data limited to lesion-growth endpoints; functional (visual acuity, dark adaptation) benefits remain to be demonstrated.

Conclusion  
Avacincaptad pegol is a well-characterized, potent C5 inhibitor with strong mechanistic rationale and encouraging early clinical data in geographic atrophy. In RPE/POS phagocytosis assays, it is expected to normalize lysosomal function and reduce inflammasome activation, making it a leading candidate for further preclinical and translational studies in dry AMD. Its strengths lie in target specificity and ocular delivery, but its ultimate utility may depend on combination strategies addressing the multifactorial nature of AMD.

Proposal for Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Proposal for AAV2-CFH gene therapy

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.  
  – AAV2-CFH gene therapy combines a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector (developed by standard triple-plasmid transfection methods; Xie et al., 2018) carrying a codon-optimized human CFH cDNA under control of an RPE-active promoter (e.g. VMD2 or CAG enhancer). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Immune Response: Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patients may reduce transduction efficiency (Mingozzi & High, 2013).  
 2. Dose Optimization: Excessive CFH expression might dysregulate systemic complement or trigger off-target effects in the choroid or retina.  
 3. Disease Heterogeneity: Dry AMD is multifactorial; complement is one axis among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. CFH alone may not halt progression in all patients.  
 4. Tissue Distribution: Secreted CFH must penetrate Bruch’s membrane effectively; age-related changes to BrM may impede diffusion.  

Conclusion  
AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Critical path forward includes optimization of vector dose and promoter choice to achieve physiologic CFH levels, assessment of neutralizing antibody prevalence, and demonstration of functional rescue in relevant animal models of GA. Given the unmet medical need in dry AMD, AAV2-CFH merits further preclinical development toward first-in-human studies.

Proposal for Rapamycin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.).  Chemically, it is a 31-membered polyketide macrolide whose structure was elucidated by X-ray crystallography and NMR.  Total syntheses and semisynthetic modifications have been reported, but the commercial drug is obtained by fermentation of S. hygroscopicus followed by chromatographic purification.  Rapamycin belongs to the class of “rapalogs” or FK506-binding protein (FKBP)–binding immunosuppressants/antiproliferatives.  Its prototypical use has been to prevent graft rejection (renal, cardiac) and, more recently, to coat coronary stents and treat certain rare pulmonary proliferative disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.  
• Lymphangioleiomyomatosis: inhibits smooth muscle–like cell proliferation in lung.  
• Ocular uses—systemic or intravitreal rapamycin has been tested in small trials for proliferative vitreoretinopathy, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, and neovascular AMD (no large phase III for dry AMD).  Safety in intravitreal injection demonstrated no gross retinal toxicity at doses achieving low-nanomolar vitreous concentrations (ImmunoGen et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical in RPE/dry AMD models: several groups have shown rapamycin upregulates autophagy and reduces lipofuscin/A2E accumulation in RPE cell lines and in vivo in mouse models of RPE stress (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/−, light-damage models).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. FKBP12 Binding: rapamycin binds the immunophilin FKBP12 to form a binary complex.  
2. mTORC1 Allosteric Inhibition: the FKBP12–rapamycin complex docks on the FRB domain of mTOR within mTORC1 (the complex containing mTOR, raptor, mLST8), disrupting substrate recruitment.  Phosphorylation of key mTORC1 targets—S6K1 (Thr389) and 4E–BP1—falls.  
3. Autophagy Induction: by relieving ULK1 from mTORC1–mediated phosphorylation, rapamycin activates the ULK1/ATG13/FIP200 complex, initiating autophagosome formation.  Concurrently, mTORC1 suppression enhances nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3, upregulating lysosomal biogenesis and CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsins).  
4. Possible mTORC2 Effects: chronic or high-dose rapamycin can disrupt mTORC2 assembly in some cell types, reducing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and affecting cell survival pathways; this is typically dose- and cell-context dependent.  

Extensive biochemical characterization of rapamycin–FKBP12–mTOR interactions has been reported (Choi et al., 1996; Sabatini et al., 1994).  In RPE models, mTOR, raptor, ULK1, LC3, p62/SQSTM1, and TFEB are all expressed (McWilliams et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assay  
Assay context: RPE cells (primary human or iPSC-derived) challenged with photoreceptor outer segments (POS) or A2E to model lipofuscin and drusen precursor accumulation.  A readout of interest is autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover +/- bafilomycin), p62 levels, lysosomal enzyme activity, and residual POS/A2E burden (fluorimetry, confocal imaging).  

Rapamycin is expected to:  
• Increase formation of LC3-positive autophagosomes and promote their fusion with lysosomes (elevated LC3-II flux; decreased p62).  
• Upregulate lysosomal gene expression via TFEB dephosphorylation, increasing cathepsin activity and LAMP1 surface.  
• Accelerate breakdown of POS-derived proteins and lipids, reducing intracellular A2E-like fluorophores.  
• Mitigate oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokine release downstream of POS overload, as mTORC1 suppression has been linked to reduced IL-1β and TNFα in RPE (Zhang et al., 2017).  

Key references:  
• Guan et al. (2015): rapamycin reduced A2E accumulation in ARPE-19 by 40% over 48 h.  
• Kim et al. (2013): knockdown of raptor phenocopies rapamycin’s enhancement of POS clearance in primary RPE.  
• Kaarniranta et al. (2016): mTOR hyperactivation correlates with drusen load in donor RPE from AMD eyes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Targets a validated node in dry AMD pathogenesis—impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance of POS debris.  mTORC1 activation has been observed in aged/diseased RPE, and genetic or pharmacologic mTORC1 suppression restores proteostasis.  
• Rapamycin is well characterized: known ocular pharmacokinetics after intravitreal injection (half-life ~60 h in rabbit vitreous), established manufacturing, stability, and dose-finding data.  
• Clinical safety profile is favorable; local administration minimizes systemic immunosuppression.  

Weaknesses / Risks  
• Rapamycin’s allosteric inhibition is partial; residual mTORC1 activity may limit maximal autophagy induction (4E-BP1 phosphorylation is less sensitive than S6K1).  
• Excessive or prolonged mTORC1 inhibition may impair RPE protein synthesis, mitochondrial biogenesis, and wound-healing responses.  Chronic dosing must balance autophagy induction versus cellular homeostasis.  
• Potential off-target effects on mTORC2 at higher or repeated doses—possible impact on AKT-mediated survival pathways in RPE.  
• Intravitreal delivery risks (e.g., endophthalmitis, steroid-associated IOP elevation if dual therapy).  

Conclusion  
Rapamycin is a strong candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, directly addressing autophagy/lysosomal deficiency in RPE.  Its known ocular PK, safety in the eye, and robust mechanistic rationale support moving into optimized in vitro RPE–POS assays and subsequent in vivo models of dry AMD.  Key next steps should include:  
1. Dose–response studies in human primary RPE to map the window between autophagy induction and adverse effects on cell viability/mitochondrial function.  
2. Comparison with ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors (e.g., Torin1) to assess whether fuller mTORC1/2 blockade offers incremental benefit or greater toxicity.  
3. Longitudinal animal studies in aging or genetic AMD models, with endpoints including drusen-like deposit formation, RPE integrity (OCT, histology), and visual function (ERG).  
4. Exploration of intermittent versus continuous dosing to maximize clearance of accumulated debris while preserving RPE anabolic functions.  

Given the preclinical data and clinical familiarity, low-dose intravitreal rapamycin merits prioritized advancement in the dry AMD therapeutic pipeline.

Proposal for Ambroxol

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol (trans-4-[(2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzyl)amino]cyclohexanol) is a small-molecule mucolytic originally synthesized in the 1970s as an active metabolite of bromhexine. Chemically, it is a lipophilic weak base (pKa ~9) that readily crosses cell membranes and accumulates in acidic compartments. Ambroxol belongs to the class of pharmacological chaperones for lysosomal enzymes: small compounds that bind and stabilize mutant or labile enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum, promoting proper folding and trafficking to the lysosome. Beyond its mucolytic use, ambroxol has attracted attention for its ability to bind and stabilize glucocerebrosidase (GCase, encoded by GBA), rescuing its activity in Gaucher disease and Parkinson’s disease models.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Mucolytic/Expectorant (Clinical decades): Approved in many countries for respiratory indications (bronchitis, cystic fibrosis) at oral or nebulized doses up to 90 mg/day. Its safety profile is well established, with mild gastrointestinal or skin reactions as the most common adverse events.  
2. Gaucher Disease & Parkinson’s Disease (Off-label/Preclinical): From ~2009 onward, multiple in vitro and in vivo studies (McNeill et al., 2014; Migdalska-Richards & Schapira, 2016; Rocha et al., 2015) demonstrated that ambroxol binds GCase, increases its lysosomal trafficking and activity, reduces substrate accumulation, and improves autophagic flux. A small open-label trial (Mistry et al., 2019) in type 1 Gaucher patients showed increased leukocyte GCase activity. Early Parkinson’s trials are ongoing.  
3. Use in Ophthalmology: No published studies to date have tested ambroxol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any primary retinal disease. However, tissue distribution models and animal PK studies indicate that systemically administered ambroxol reaches the retina and vitreous at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (≤1–10 µM), warranting exploration in retinal degenerations characterized by lysosomal dysfunction.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Pharmacological Chaperone of GCase: Ambroxol binds directly to the catalytic domain of GCase at neutral pH (Kd ~0.5–5 µM), stabilizing its folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sawkar et al., 2006; Maegawa et al., 2009). This facilitates ER exit and trafficking via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to the late endosome/lysosome.  
2. Lysosomal Activity Enhancement: Once in the lysosome, ambroxol dissociates from GCase in the acidic environment, allowing GCase to hydrolyze glucosylceramide into ceramide and glucose. In patient-derived fibroblasts and neurons, ambroxol elevates residual GCase activity by 30–100%, reduces glucosylceramide storage, and restores autophagic flux (Rocha et al., 2015; Migdalska-Richards et al., 2017).  
3. Lysosomal Biogenesis and Acidification: Several studies (Song et al., 2013; Parenti et al., 2014) report that ambroxol upregulates TFEB (transcription factor EB), the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, leading to increased expression of lysosomal proteins (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsin D) and enhanced lysosomal acidification.  
4. Anti-Inflammatory and Anti-Oxidative Effects: In respiratory models ambroxol suppresses NF-κB activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), scavenges ROS, and stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential—effects that may be relevant in the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2012).  

Expected Effect in RPE POS-Degradation Assay  
Proposed assay: human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) pulsed with photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and quantifying lysosomal processing over 24–48 h.  
1. GCase in RPE: Public transcriptome and proteome datasets (Zhao et al., 2011; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm robust expression of GBA and GCase protein in RPE, localizing to LAMP1+ lysosomes.  
2. Hypothesis Testing: Ambroxol (1–10 µM) pretreatment should increase GCase activity (measured by 4-MUG substrate assay) and enhance co-localization of POS markers (rhodopsin) with lysosomal markers (LAMP1/CTSD) at early time points (2–6 h), reduce accumulation of POS-derived autofluorescent lipofuscin bisretinoids (A2E) at 48 h, and increase cathepsin D and LC3-II turnover as readouts of improved autophagic flux.  
3. Lysosomal pH: Using pH-sensitive probes (LysoSensor), ambroxol should correct any pathology-associated alkalinization of the lysosome in an oxidative environment, thereby optimizing hydrolase function.  
4. Downstream Readouts: Reduced reactive oxygen species (DCFDA), decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and preserved mitochondrial potential (JC-1) in RPE under chronic POS challenge.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Lysosomal dysfunction and impaired POS degradation are core features in dry AMD pathology (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaemmerer et al., 2017). Ambroxol directly targets GCase folding/activity and boosts general lysosomal capacity via TFEB, addressing upstream defects rather than downstream inflammation only.  
• Safety and Pharmacokinetics: Decades of clinical use for respiratory disease demonstrate safety at systemic exposures likely to achieve retinal concentrations (1–10 µM). Lipophilicity and basicity favor lysosomal accumulation in RPE.  
• Precedent in Neurodegeneration: Successful proof-of-concept in Gaucher and Parkinson’s disease supports translational potential in another lysosome-dependent tissue.  
Weaknesses/Risks  
• Off-Target Effects: As a lysosomotropic agent, ambroxol may alter pH in other cellular compartments; high concentrations can cause lysosomal swelling or compromised membrane integrity in some cell types (Mazzulli et al., 2016).  
• Efficacy Margin: Degree of GCase upregulation in wild-type cells may be modest (20–40%), and dry AMD is a multifactorial disease—lysosomal enhancement alone may not fully prevent RPE atrophy.  
• Chronic Dosing: Dry AMD requires long-term therapy; chronic administration risks tolerability issues or tachyphylaxis. Local delivery (intravitreal or periocular) may be needed but requires formulation development.  
Conclusion  
Ambroxol is a well-characterized pharmacological chaperone of GCase with additional lysosomal biogenesis and anti-inflammatory effects. Its mechanism directly addresses RPE lysosomal impairment, the nexus of POS debris accumulation and lipofuscin formation in dry AMD. The compound’s safety profile and achievable retinal penetration make it a strong candidate for repurposing. The primary risks are modest efficacy in wild-type settings, potential off-target lysosomal perturbations, and the need for chronic ocular delivery strategies. We recommend proceeding to in vitro RPE-POS assays to quantify ambroxol’s enhancement of GCase activity, lysosomal pH correction, and POS clearance, followed by in vivo dosing studies in AMD rodent or primate models before clinical translation.

Proposal for Anakinra (IL-1R antagonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic specificity: Targets a well-validated pathogenic axis in dry AMD (Alu RNA → NLRP3 → IL-1β → lysosomal damage).  
2. Clinical precedence: FDA-approved, known safety profile, rapid repurposing potential.  
3. Readily assayable: Effects on inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage), IL-1β secretion (ELISA), lysosomal integrity (acridine orange or cathepsin assays), and POS uptake can be quantitatively measured in standard RPE culture models.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Delivery to the retina: Systemic anakinra has limited blood-retinal barrier penetration; intravitreal or periocular dosing would require new formulation and safety testing.  
2. Short half-life in ocular tissues: May need frequent dosing or sustained-release delivery to maintain effective blockade.  
3. Incomplete pathway coverage: IL-1β is only one downstream mediator of NLRP3 activation; other inflammasome effectors (e.g., IL-18, pyroptotic pore formation) may continue to drive RPE damage.  
4. Potential off-target immunosuppression: Chronic IL-1 blockade could increase susceptibility to ocular or systemic infections.  

Conclusion  
Anakinra is a biologically and clinically plausible candidate for blocking IL-1β–mediated inflammasome amplification and preserving lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE—key pathomechanisms in dry AMD. Its prior approval and mechanistic specificity support rapid translation, but challenges around ocular delivery, dosing frequency, and complete pathway suppression will need to be addressed in preclinical models before moving toward clinical trials.

Proposal for Fenofibrate

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.  
• Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. Preclinical wet AMD models have occasionally used PPARα agonists to attenuate choroidal neovascularization, but studies in geographic atrophy or RPE degeneration models are very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Upregulation of FAO and ketogenesis: Key target genes include CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD, ACADL, and HMGCS2. These enzymes increase mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body synthesis.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: PPARα activation transrepresses NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, reducing expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and adhesion molecules.  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE and RPE-like cell lines (ARPE-19) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Xiao et al., 2003; Perepechaeva et al., 2013). PPARα activation in RPE cultures enhances mitochondrial respiration and protects against oxidative stress.  
• POS phagocytosis link: Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis is an energy-intensive, ATP-dependent process. Studies (Young & Knox, 2014) show that boosting RPE fatty acid catabolism improves phagocytic clearance of POS, reduces lipofuscin accumulation, and supports RPE homeostasis.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
In an in vitro assay measuring RPE phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled POS, fenofibrate (or fenofibric acid) is expected to:  
1) Increase expression of FAO enzymes (CPT1A, ACOX1) and ketogenesis enzymes (HMGCS2), measurable by qPCR or Western blot within 24–48 h of treatment (Huang et al., 2015).  
2) Elevate mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and spare respiratory capacity in Seahorse assays, indicating enhanced β-oxidation (Perepechaeva et al., 2013).  
3) Boost intracellular ATP levels, detectable by luminescence assays, especially after POS challenge.  
4) Increase the rate and total uptake of POS in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures, assessable by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Young & Knox, 2014).  
5) Reduce accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin precursors over prolonged treatment.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Strong preclinical evidence that PPARα activation augments RPE metabolic capacity and phagocytosis, directly addressing energy deficits implicated in dry AMD.  
• Safety and PK: Fenofibrate has decades of human safety data, well-characterized pharmacokinetics, generic availability, and known drug–drug interactions.  
• Dual lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory actions: May also ameliorate subclinical inflammation and lipid drusen formation in the sub-RPE space.  
Weaknesses  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing leads to low fenofibric acid concentrations in the posterior eye; unknown whether therapeutic concentrations can be achieved in RPE. Intravitreal delivery poses formulation and safety challenges.  
• PPARα dependency: Genetic variability in PPARα polymorphisms may influence response; PPARα expression declines with age in RPE (Zhao et al., 2017).  
• Lack of AMD-specific data: No published in vivo models specifically testing fenofibrate in geographic atrophy or drusen accumulation. Translation from diabetic retinopathy benefit to dry AMD is not guaranteed.  
• Potential off-target lipid effects: Systemic lipid modulation may have unintended consequences in elderly AMD patients who may be normolipidemic.  

Conclusion  
Fenofibrate is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its PPARα-driven enhancement of RPE fatty acid oxidation and phagocytic function, backed by extensive safety data. Key next steps include:  
1) Demonstrating dose–response for fenofibric acid in RPE POS‐phagocytosis assays and mitochondrial function assays.  
2) Assessing intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations to overcome ocular penetration barriers.  
3) Testing in animal models of RPE atrophy/drusen (e.g., sodium iodate or complement factor H knock-in mice).  
4) Investigating patient stratification based on PPARα expression or activity.  
Given its mechanistic alignment and existing clinical safety profile, fenofibrate merits further preclinical development for dry AMD.

Proposal for GKT137831 (NOX1/4 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.  

Conclusion  
GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models. A focused program of RPE cell–based assays, ocular PK studies in rodents or rabbits, and evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, Abca4−/−Rdh8−/− phototoxicity) would be the next logical steps to determine viability for clinical repurposing.

Proposal for Iptacopan (LNP023, Factor B inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). It belongs to the class of peptidomimetic complement inhibitors targeting serine proteases of the alternative pathway (AP). Small-molecule AP inhibitors have been explored for indications in which chronic AP overactivation drives pathology (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy).

Therapeutic History  
– Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Iptacopan is in late-stage clinical trials (Phase III) for PNH, where oral FB inhibition reduces hemolysis and transfusion needs with a favorable safety profile (No significant infections or thromboses).  
– C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published preclinical or clinical studies of iptacopan in dry AMD or other retinal diseases. By contrast, other AP inhibitors such as anti-factor D (lampalizumab) and anti-C3 (pegcetacoplan) have reached AMD trials—with mixed or negative outcomes—highlighting both the validity and challenges of complement targeting in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.  
– Iptacopan binds the active-site cleft of factor B, stabilizing it in an inactive conformation and preventing Bb generation. Crystallography (PDB entries for FB-iptacopan complexes) shows hydrogen bonds to the S1 pocket and van der Waals contacts that confer high selectivity over other complement proteases (factor D, C1s).  
– By blocking AP C3 convertase assembly, it reduces C3b “tick-over” amplification loops without directly inhibiting the classical or lectin pathways. This preserves systemic immune competence while attenuating local complement-driven inflammation.

Expected Effect in RPE/Choroid Cell-Culture Assay  
– RPE and choroidal endothelial cells are known to synthesize FB and other complement components (Anderson et al., 2010; Bora et al., 2005). Genetic studies (CFH, CFB risk alleles) and proteomic analyses of drusen contain elevated FB, C3b, and MAC.  
– In an in vitro co-culture of human iPSC-derived RPE plus choroidal endothelial cells, activation of AP (e.g., via oxidative stress or sublytic C5b-9 exposure) leads to lysosomal dysfunction and impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
– Addition of iptacopan is expected to (1) reduce deposition of C3b and sublytic MAC on RPE basal surfaces, (2) preserve lysosomal acidification and degradation capacity (tracked by LysoTracker and DQ-BSA assays), and (3) restore or maintain POS phagocytosis (measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  
– Literature support: Lampalizumab (anti-FD) prevented MAC formation and preserved RPE viability under complement stress (e.g., Lyzenga et al., 2018). Given FB sits upstream of FD, iptacopan may achieve wider reduction in C3b amplification.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with AMD genetics: FB inhibition directly targets the overactive AP amplification loop implicated by CFH, CFB, and C3 risk variants.  
• Oral dosing and favorable systemic safety in PNH/C3G trials suggest manageable risk.  
• Selectivity for AP minimizes impact on classical/lectin pathways, reducing infection risk versus broad C3 or C5 inhibitors.  
• Precedent of small-molecule complement inhibitors enables formulation flexibility; potential to test both systemic and localized delivery (e.g., periocular).

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Human retinal penetration after oral dosing is not yet published; drug concentrations in RPE/choroid must reach IC₅₀ (~5–20 nM) for FB.  
• Alternative pathway redundancy: Local complement regulators (e.g., CFH) are reduced in AMD; whether FB blockade alone suffices to normalize complement control in the subretinal space remains unproven.  
• Previous complement trials in AMD have failed (e.g., lampalizumab) possibly due to patient selection or insufficient target engagement; iptacopan must demonstrate robust local C3b and MAC suppression in vivo.  
• Long-term complement suppression risks: chronic FB inhibition may alter retinal homeostasis and microbiome, and eye-specific immunity.

Conclusion  
Iptacopan is mechanistically compelling for dry AMD due to its targeted blockade of the AP amplification loop, favorable systemic safety, and robust preclinical efficacy in other complement-driven diseases. Critical next steps include quantitative retinal pharmacokinetics (ocular distribution after oral or periocular dosing), ex vivo human RPE/choroid tissue assays to confirm local target engagement, and selection of AMD patient genotypes (e.g., CFB risk carriers) for future proof-of-concept studies.

Proposal for Elamipretide (SS-31)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. Specifically:  
• SS-31 binding inhibits cardiolipin peroxidation by shielding its polyunsaturated fatty acid tails, thereby reducing lipid-derived ROS.  
• It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.  
These actions collectively improve mitochondrial respiration (measured as increased oxygen consumption rate [OCR] and spare respiratory capacity) and reduce apoptosis under oxidative or nutrient-stress conditions.

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD–relevant assays often employ primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cells challenged with oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) or with isolated photoreceptor outer segments (POS) labeled for phagocytosis. Key RPE‐expressed mitochondrial genes such as CRLS1 (cardiolipin synthase), CYC1 (cytochrome c1), CYCS (cytochrome c) and ATP5A1 (ATP synthase α) are robustly transcribed in RPE (RNA-seq data, EyeIntegration database). In stressed RPE:  
1. SS-31 (0.1–10 μM) is expected to localize to mitochondria within 30 minutes of addition (based on live-cell imaging with fluorescent SS-31 analogs).  
2. It should decrease mitochondrial ROS (detectable by MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays) and improve mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 assay).  
3. It should increase basal and maximal OCR (Seahorse XF analysis) and elevate cellular ATP content (luminescence assay).  
4. Enhanced bioenergetics provides more ATP for the energy-intensive process of POS phagocytosis, measurable as increased uptake of FITC- or pHrodo-labeled POS over 4–6 hours.  
5. Secondary benefits may include reduced RPE cell death (Annexin V/PI staining) and preservation of ZO-1 tight junction integrity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct targeting of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction—a recognized contributor to dry AMD pathogenesis—offers a clear, hypothesis-driven approach.  
• Preclinical Validation: Robust data in multiple tissue models demonstrate improvements in mitochondrial morphology, oxidative stress and ATP production.  
• Safety Profile: Early-phase clinical trials in non-ocular indications and an open-label ocular study report good tolerability.  
• Feasibility: SS-31 is water-soluble and cell-permeable, obviating the need for complex delivery vehicles.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Delivery and Dosing: Intravitreal or topical routes have limited published data on retinal bioavailability and pharmacokinetics; systemic delivery may not achieve therapeutic levels in RPE.  
• Limited AMD-Specific Data: No randomized clinical trial has yet demonstrated efficacy in dry AMD; preclinical RPE-specific studies remain sparse.  
• Multifactorial Pathogenesis: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipofuscin accumulation and extracellular deposit formation; mitochondrial rescue alone may be insufficient for disease modification.  
• Long-Term Effects: Chronic administration could have unforeseen effects on mitochondrial dynamics or innate immunity in the eye.

Conclusion  
Elamipretide (SS-31) is a well-characterized, mitochondrial‐targeting peptide with strong mechanistic justification for addressing RPE bioenergetic deficits in dry AMD. Its ability to stabilize cardiolipin, restore cristae architecture, reduce ROS and boost ATP aligns directly with current hypotheses on RPE failure in AMD. Key next steps should include optimization of ocular delivery (e.g., sustained-release intravitreal formulations), detailed in vitro phagocytosis assays, and in vivo efficacy studies in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Cfh−/− or Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice) to build a robust preclinical package before proceeding to pivotal human trials.

Proposal for Melatonin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenously produced indoleamine synthesized in the pineal gland from serotonin via arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) (Hardeland et al., 2006). First isolated in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958), it belongs to the class of small-molecule pleiotropic neurohormones. Exogenous melatonin is manufactured by chemical synthesis, typically via O-methylation of 5-hydroxytryptamine followed by N-acetylation. As a therapeutic class, indoleamines have been used primarily for sleep regulation, jet-lag, circadian rhythm disorders, and as systemic antioxidants.

Therapeutic History  
•  General human use: approved over-the-counter for insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep disorders at doses between 0.5 and 10 mg (Zisapel, 2018).  
•  Antioxidant/anti-inflammatory: evaluated in neurodegenerative disorders (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) for its ROS-scavenging and mitochondrial protective properties (Reiter et al., 2000; Cardinali et al., 2010).  
•  Retinal protection: shown to prevent light-induced photoreceptor loss in rodent models (Ma et al., 2012) and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration (Li et al., 2019).  
•  Clinical studies in AMD: no registered clinical trials using melatonin for dry AMD; a single small open-label study (n = 20) suggested stabilized visual acuity with oral melatonin but lacked controls (“Unpublished conference abstract,” 2015).

Mechanism of Action  
1.  Receptor-mediated signaling  
    •  Melatonin binds GPCRs MT1 (MTNR1A) and MT2 (MTNR1B) with nanomolar affinity (Chong & Sugden, 1994). MT1/MT2 are expressed in human RPE and photoreceptors (Stauch et al., 2016; Idriss et al., 2020).  
    •  Activation of MT1/MT2 inhibits adenylate cyclase via Gi proteins, reducing cAMP, modulating downstream PKA/CREB pathways (Dubocovich, 2007). In RPE, this signaling upregulates antioxidant defenses (Gueron et al., 2016).  
2.  Mitochondrial actions  
    •  A mitochondrial localization of MT1 has been described on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where melatonin counteracts Ca²⁺-induced permeability transition pore opening and prevents cytochrome c release (Franco et al., 2011).  
    •  Receptor-independent: directly scavenges hydroxyl, peroxyl, and singlet oxygen species; stimulates expression/activity of SOD, GPx, and catalase (Tan et al., 1999).  
3.  Mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover  
    •  Melatonin enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neuronal and hepatic cells, via SIRT3 activation and FoxO3a deacetylation (Kwon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).  
    •  In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin treatment increased LC3II accumulation, decreased p62, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Gueron et al., 2016).  
4.  Phagocytosis support  
    •  ATP generated from healthy mitochondria fuels αvβ5- and MERTK-mediated engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Mazzoni et al., 2014). Melatonin-driven mitochondrial preservation may thus enhance POS clearance.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
In an in vitro RPE culture assay (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE):  
•  Antioxidant protection: melatonin (0.1–10 µM) is expected to reduce H₂O₂-induced ROS (DCF fluorescence) by ≥ 40 % after 24 h (Gueron et al., 2016).  
•  Mitophagy activation: increased Parkin recruitment to mitochondria (immunofluorescence) and elevated LC3II/p62 flux (western blot) within 12 h treatment at 5 µM (Zhang et al., 2016).  
•  Mitochondrial function: preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 assay) and ATP levels (luminescent assay) following oxidative challenge (Franco et al., 2011).  
•  POS phagocytosis: enhanced uptake of FITC-labeled POS by ≥ 25 % over vehicle, mediated by ATP support (as in Mazzoni et al., 2014). Expression of MTNR1A/B in RPE confirmed by qPCR (Idriss et al., 2020) supports receptor-dependent effects.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Strong mechanistic rationale targeting two critical AMD pathways: oxidative mitochondrial injury and defective POS clearance.  
•  Extensive safety record in humans; well-characterized PK with favorable blood-retina penetration (Back et al., 2010).  
•  Dual receptor-mediated and direct antioxidant effects reduce risk of target resistance.

Weaknesses  
•  Endogenous melatonin levels decline with age and in AMD patients, potentially limiting receptor availability (Yang et al., 2021).  
•  Rapid first-pass metabolism (t½ ≈ 30 min) may require sustained-release formulation to maintain therapeutic retinal concentrations.  
•  Possible receptor desensitization with chronic high-dose use.

Conclusion  
Melatonin is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with multimodal actions on RPE mitochondrial health and phagocytic capacity. Key next steps include dose-response optimization in RPE assays, development of retinal-targeted delivery systems, and validation of functional endpoints (mitophagy flux, POS clearance) before in vivo efficacy studies.

Proposal for PMX205 (C5aR antagonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PMX205 is a synthetic cyclic hexapeptide antagonist of the complement 5a receptor (C5aR, CD88). It was derived by structure–activity optimization of the earlier peptide antagonist PMX53, incorporating non-proteinogenic amino acids and a cyclization scaffold to improve metabolic stability, receptor affinity, and oral bioavailability. PMX205 belongs to the class of small-molecule/peptidomimetic complement inhibitors targeting G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling. Compounds of this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory agents in diseases where excessive complement activation drives pathology (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, neuroinflammation).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: PMX205 (and its predecessor PMX53) have been tested in multiple rodent models of inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease—including Alzheimer’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and ischemia–reperfusion injury—where blockade of C5aR reduced microglial activation, cytokine release (IL-1β, TNF-α), and tissue damage.  
• Pharmacokinetics/Toxicology: Compared to PMX53, PMX205 shows improved half-life after oral dosing, higher tissue penetration (including brain and eye tissues), and a favorable safety profile in rodents, with no overt immunosuppression at efficacious doses.  
• Clinical status: To date, no completed Phase I–III trials of PMX205 in humans have been published. Related C5aR antagonists (e.g., avacopan, vilobelimab) have advanced in other indications, validating the receptor as a druggable target.  
• Use in ocular disease: There are no reports of direct PMX205 use in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, C5aR blockade has been proposed as a strategy in dry AMD by multiple groups, and complement inhibitors (C3, C5 antibodies) are in clinical trials for geographic atrophy.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: PMX205 binds with high affinity to the C5aR1 (CD88) binding pocket, acting as a competitive antagonist that prevents the pro-inflammatory anaphylatoxin C5a from activating its GPCR.  
• Downstream signaling: In the absence of C5aR1 activation, intracellular Ca2+ flux, MAPK (ERK1/2, p38) phosphorylation, NF-κB nuclear translocation, and NLRP3 inflammasome priming are reduced in myeloid and epithelial cells. This suppresses activation of caspase-1 and maturation/secretion of IL-1β and IL-18.  
• Impact on RPE/Phagolysosomes: Published studies in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE) document expression of C5aR1. C5a exposure in vitro induces lysosomal alkalinization, reduced cathepsin D processing, accumulation of undigested photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material, and NLRP3 activation. By preventing C5a/C5aR1 engagement, PMX205 is expected to restore lysosomal acidification, hydrolytic enzyme activity, and effective POS clearance.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assays  
In an in vitro RPE assay combining oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2 or blue-light exposure), complement activation (addition of recombinant human C5a or serum with activated complement), and POS feeding:  
• PMX205 should dose-dependently inhibit C5a-mediated Ca2+ influx (IC50 in low nM range).  
• It should reduce expression of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, cleavage of caspase-1 (p20 fragment), and secretion of mature IL-1β/IL-18 (reportable by ELISA).  
• Restoration of lysosomal pH can be assayed with LysoTracker or pH-sensitive probes, and cathepsin D activity monitored with fluorogenic substrates.  
• POS uptake and degradation can be quantified by immunofluorescence or flow cytometry; PMX205 should normalize the rate of rhodopsin clearance relative to untreated, complement-challenged controls.  
• Viability assays (e.g., MTT, LDH release) should show improved RPE survival under complement-driven stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: C5a/C5aR1–driven inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction are well documented in dry AMD pathogenesis. Targeting this axis addresses both inflammation and RPE clearance impairment.  
• Preclinical Validation: Robust data exist for PMX205 (and analogs) in inflammatory/neurodegenerative models, including ocular tissue penetration.  
• Drug-like Properties: Oral bioavailability, favorable PK, and safety in animal studies support feasibility of systemic dosing or potential formulation for intraocular delivery.  
• Rapid Translation: PMX205 is a repurposing candidate; synthetic route and formulation are established, facilitating IND-enabling studies.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular Exposure: Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space; local delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) may be required and entail formulation challenges.  
• Immunocompromise: Chronic complement blockade can increase susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria; risk–benefit must be assessed, particularly in elderly patients.  
• Redundancy and Compensation: Complement system has multiple receptors (C5aR2) and cross-talk with other inflammatory pathways; C5aR1 antagonism alone may be insufficient.  
• Lack of Direct Clinical Data: No existing trials in AMD; efficacy in human RPE/retina remains to be demonstrated.  

Conclusion  
PMX205 represents a highly rational, mechanism-focused candidate for dry AMD based on strong preclinical evidence linking C5aR1 signaling to RPE dysfunction and inflammation. Key next steps would include in vitro confirmation of target engagement and functional rescue in RPE/POS assays, PK studies of ocular distribution, and assessment of immunological safety in relevant animal models. If these studies are supportive, PMX205 merits advancement toward a first-in-eye proof-of-concept study.
