Proposal for Nicotinamide riboside (NR)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Chemically, it consists of a nicotinamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors (alongside nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide mononucleotide). These precursors have long been used as nutritional supplements to support cellular metabolism and redox homeostasis. NR is distinguished by high oral bioavailability and the ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels more efficiently than equivalent doses of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid, likely because it bypasses rate-limiting steps in the salvage pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• General uses of NAD⁺ precursors: nicotinic acid (niacin) has been used for decades to treat dyslipidemia; nicotinamide has been used as an over-the-counter supplement.  
• NR in preclinical models: efficacy demonstrated in models of metabolic disease (obesity, insulin resistance), neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s), muscular dystrophy, and age-related muscle decline.  
• Clinical trials in humans: multiple small studies (200–2,000 mg/day NR for up to 12 weeks) have confirmed safety, tolerability, and significant elevation of NAD⁺ in blood cells without serious adverse events. Improvements in markers of mitochondrial function and inflammation have been reported in elderly volunteers.  
• Use in ocular disease: no published trials of NR in dry AMD or other retinal dystrophies to date. A few preclinical studies in retinopathy models suggest NAD⁺ augmentation can protect photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells from light or oxidative stress, but direct studies in RPE or AMD models remain very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Biosynthesis and Sirtuin Activation  
   – NR is phosphorylated by NRKs to yield nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), then converted by NMN adenylyltransferases to NAD⁺.  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor for sirtuin deacylases (SIRT1–SIRT7). In the RPE context, SIRT1 and SIRT3 are most relevant:  
     • SIRT1 (nuclear/cytosolic) deacetylates transcription factors (PGC-1α) to promote mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant gene expression, and autophagy gene transcription.  
     • SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates enzymes in the TCA cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

2. Autophagy and POS Clearance  
   – Aging RPE cells exhibit impaired macroautophagy and phagolysosome maturation, leading to suboptimal photoreceptor outer segment (POS) turnover.  
   – SIRT1 activation upregulates autophagy-related proteins (LC3, ATG5/7) and enhances TFEB (master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Animal and cell studies show that boosting NAD⁺ can restore autophagic flux in aged cells.

3. Mitochondrial Function and Oxidative Stress  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for key dehydrogenases in glycolysis, TCA cycle, and fatty acid oxidation. Higher NAD⁺/NADH ratio improves mitochondrial respiration.  
   – SIRT3-mediated deacetylation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2) reduces ROS accumulation.

4. Inflammation and Complement Regulation  
   – NAD⁺ levels modulate the NLRP3 inflammasome via SIRT2 and SIRT6. In RPE, chronic inflammasome activation and complement dysregulation contribute to drusen formation. Elevated NAD⁺ may dampen inflammatory cytokine release (IL-1β, IL-18).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
Assay readouts might include:  
• Intracellular NAD⁺ quantification (by cycling assay or LC-MS) – expected 2–5 fold increase with 0.1–1 mM NR in cultured RPE.  
• Sirtuin activity (fluorometric deacetylation assays for SIRT1/SIRT3 substrates).  
• Autophagic flux (LC3-II/I ratio, p62 degradation, tandem mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporter).  
• POS phagocytosis and clearance (fluorescently labeled rod outer segments; measure uptake and degradation kinetics).  
• Mitochondrial respiration (Seahorse OCR assays) – expect increased basal and maximal respiration, spare capacity.  
• ROS levels (MitoSOX or DCFDA) – expect reduction in both basal and induced ROS.  
• Inflammatory markers (qPCR/ELISA for IL-1β, C3 complement factor).

Mechanistic linkage: RPE expresses NRK1/2, SIRT1, SIRT3, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery. Multiple transcriptomic datasets (e.g., Human Protein Atlas, GEO RPE‐specific studies) confirm these gene products are abundant in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Strong mechanistic rationale: addresses two key dry AMD pathologies—impaired POS clearance via autophagy defects and mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—through a single intervention.  
• Well‐tolerated in humans at doses likely sufficient to modulate RPE NAD⁺ (oral NR up to 2 g/day raises systemic NAD⁺; bioavailability to retina plausible given preclinical evidence in other neural tissues).  
• Multi‐modal: indirectly modulates inflammation and complement activity, potentially impacting drusen formation.  
• Off‐patent or low‐cost nutritional supplement, facilitating rapid translation and low regulatory barrier.

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Retinal bioavailability: Few studies have directly measured NR or NAD⁺ elevation in the RPE/choroid after oral dosing. Blood‐retina barrier penetration and local metabolism need characterization.  
• Dose and regimen optimization: effective concentrations in vitro (0.5–1 mM) may not correlate directly to achievable in vivo retinal exposure.  
• Long‐term efficacy: dry AMD is chronic; whether sustained NR supplementation can slow geographic atrophy progression remains untested.  
• Off‐target effects: systemic NAD⁺ elevation may affect other sirtuins or PARPs, with potential metabolic consequences or interference with complement regulation outside the eye.  
• Lack of AMD-specific preclinical data: no published in vivo models of dry AMD treated with NR; bridging studies (e.g., in aging mice with RPE degeneration or complement dysregulation) are needed.

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide riboside is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with solid mechanistic underpinnings in NAD⁺ biology, sirtuin activation, and autophagy enhancement. The oral safety profile and existing human NAD⁺ data accelerate its translational potential. Key next steps include (1) pharmacokinetic studies to confirm RPE/NAD⁺ elevation in vivo, (2) efficacy testing in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Cfh–/–, Alu RNA–induced RPE atrophy), and (3) dose-finding biomarker trials in early dry AMD patients using noninvasive retinal imaging and tear/aqueous humor NAD⁺ markers.

Proposal for Astaxanthin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Astaxanthin is a naturally occurring keto-carotenoid first identified in the microalga Haematococcus pluvialis and also found in yeast (Phaffia rhodozyma), salmon, shrimp, and krill. Commercially, it is obtained either by cultivation of H. pluvialis under stress conditions that induce astaxanthin accumulation or by chemical synthesis starting from β-ionone or from zeaxanthin via oxidative ring closure. Structurally, astaxanthin (3,3′-dihydroxy-β,β-carotene-4,4′-dione) belongs to the xanthophyll subclass of carotenoids, distinguished by polar end groups (hydroxyl and keto moieties) that confer both lipophilicity and membrane-spanning orientation. Carotenoids have long been used as dietary supplements (e.g., β-carotene, lutein, zeaxanthin) for their antioxidant and pro-vitamin A properties, and xanthophylls in particular have been investigated for eye health.

Therapeutic History  
• Dietary supplement and nutraceutical: Astaxanthin has been marketed for skin health, endurance exercise, cardiovascular support, and eye health. Typical oral doses range from 4–12 mg/day.  
• Preclinical ophthalmic studies: In rodent and rabbit models, astaxanthin protected against light-induced retinal damage, reduced lipid peroxidation in the retina, and preserved electrophysiological function (ERG amplitudes).  
• Clinical studies in humans:  
   – A small randomized trial (N ≈ 25) in adults with early AMD or age-related eye fatigue reported improvements in critical flicker fusion frequency, visual acuity, and macular pigment optical density after 8–12 weeks of 6 mg/day astaxanthin plus lutein/zeaxanthin (Khan et al., 2010; Eggebeen et al., 2013).  
   – Several open-label studies in myopic and healthy subjects showed improved accommodation and contrast sensitivity.  
• Use in related pathologies: Astaxanthin has been studied in models of diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and uveitis for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Dry AMD: To date no large-scale, placebo-controlled trial has evaluated astaxanthin monotherapy in dry AMD, though it has been included as part of multi-nutrient formulations (with vitamins C & E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) explored in small pilot studies.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Lipid peroxyl radical scavenging: Astaxanthin’s conjugated polyene chain neutralizes singlet oxygen and peroxyl radicals with rate constants (k) up to 10^8–10^9 M^–1·s^–1, exceeding those of β-carotene and lutein (Hussein et al., 2006). By residing across lipid bilayers, it traps radicals at the membrane interior, preventing chain-propagating lipid peroxidation.  
2. Singlet oxygen quenching: The keto and hydroxyl groups facilitate intersystem crossing and energy dissipation as heat, quenching ^1O_2 efficiently (quantum yield φ_Δ ≈ 0.5).  
3. Modulation of redox-sensitive transcription factors: In vitro, astaxanthin activates Nrf2 nuclear translocation, upregulating phase II detoxifying and antioxidant enzymes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC) (Zhu et al., 2015). It also inhibits NF-κB activation and downstream pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) in retinal and microglial cells.  
4. Mitochondrial protection: Astaxanthin preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), reduces cytochrome c release, and limits caspase-3 activation in oxidative stress models, suggesting a role in preventing RPE apoptosis.  
5. Lysosomal stabilization: By attenuating lipid peroxidation of lysosomal membranes, astaxanthin may preserve lysosomal pH and enzyme activity (cathepsins), facilitating photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation.  

Mechanistic relevance to RPE: Primary human and ARPE-19 cells express Nrf2 and NF-κB, have high mitochondrial content, and rely on robust lysosomal clearance pathways for POS turnover, making them appropriate targets for astaxanthin’s multi-modal action.

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
Assay: RPE monolayers (primary human or ARPE-19) challenged with oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂ or A2E + blue light) and then tested for POS phagocytosis and degradation.  

Astaxanthin is expected to:  
• Incorporate into RPE plasma and lysosomal membranes over 24–48 h (lipophilicity supports membrane partitioning).  
• Reduce formation of lipid peroxidation products (malondialdehyde, 4-hydroxynonenal) as measured by TBARS or immunodetection of 4-HNE adducts.  
• Preserve lysosomal acidity (LysoTracker fluorescence) and cathepsin D activity, enhancing clearance of fluorescently labeled POS.  
• Lower intracellular lipofuscin accumulation (A2E autofluorescence) in long-term feeder assays.  
• Reduce stress-induced apoptosis (Annexin V/PI, caspase 3/7 assays).  
• Activate Nrf2 target genes (qPCR or Western blot for HO-1, NQO1) and suppress NF-κB signaling (p65 phosphorylation).  

Overall, one would measure improved POS degradation kinetics (e.g., time-course of rhodopsin turnover), reduced oxidative damage markers, and enhanced RPE viability compared to untreated controls.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Multi-modal antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions targeting key pathogenic axes in dry AMD (drusen lipid peroxidation, RPE oxidative damage, lysosomal dysfunction).  
• Demonstrated ocular bioavailability after oral dosing; safety established up to 12 mg/day in humans with minimal adverse effects.  
• Potential to synergize with other AREDS2 nutrients (lutein, zeaxanthin, zinc).  
• Mechanistic rationale aligns with preservation of RPE function and POS clearance, core deficits in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Oral bioavailability and tissue delivery are limited by its lipophilicity and first-pass metabolism; nano- or microemulsion formulations may be required to reach therapeutic retinal levels.  
• Lack of large, well-controlled clinical trials specifically in dry AMD. Existing data derive from mixed-nutrient formulations or small pilot studies.  
• Long-term safety at higher doses (>12 mg/day) untested; theoretical risk of pro-oxidant activity at supraphysiological concentrations.  
• Variable response depending on genetic background (e.g., CFH, ARMS2 polymorphisms) and baseline antioxidant status may complicate patient selection.  

Conclusion  
Astaxanthin is a compelling candidate for early-stage evaluation in RPE-based assays of dry AMD given its potent membrane-targeted antioxidant properties, lysosomal stabilization, and signaling effects on redox homeostasis. Key next steps include optimizing formulation for RPE delivery, defining dose–response in in vitro POS clearance assays, and, if results are favorable, advancing to in vivo dry AMD models (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice) before designing a rigorously controlled human trial.

Proposal for Ebselen (GPX mimic)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
   – By scavenging ROS at the lysosomal membrane, ebselen preserves V-ATPase integrity and maintains acidic pH, allowing normal cathepsin-mediated proteolysis of POS (Tanito et al., 2017).

4. Indirect Effects on Lipofuscin Accumulation  
   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Culture Assay  
Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

1. Antioxidant Protection  
   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

2. Lysosomal pH Normalization  
   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation  
   – Increased rate of POS proteolysis: ~40% faster clearance of rhodopsin fragments at 24 h compared to untreated controls (Tanito et al., 2017).  
   – Cathepsin D activity assays show a 1.5-fold increase in enzymatic rate in ebselen-treated RPE over stressed controls (Li et al., 2015).

4. Gene Expression Relevance  
   – Human RPE cells (ARPE-19) and primary fetal RPE express high levels of GPX1 and GPX4 mRNA (confirmed by qPCR; GPX1 Ct ∼22, GPX4 Ct ∼24) and express V-ATPase subunits V0a1 and V1B2 required for lysosomal acidification (Hu et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic Alignment: Ebselen directly addresses two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE: oxidative lipid damage and lysosomal dysfunction.  
– Preclinical Ocular Data: Animal models and RPE cell studies show reductions in lipofuscin and preserved phagolysosomal function.  
– Safety Profile: Human Phase II data support oral safety; topical application in the eye was well tolerated in animal studies.

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– Retinal Bioavailability: Systemic dosing for sufficient retinal tissue levels remains uncharacterized; blood–retina barrier penetration needs quantification.  
– Chronic Dosing Concerns: Long-term selenium accumulation/toxicity must be evaluated, particularly in aged patients.  
– Off-Target Effects: Thiol reactivity may disrupt essential cysteine residues on other ocular proteins (e.g., crystallins), potentially leading to unforeseen toxicity.  
– Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No current human trials in dry AMD to confirm translational efficacy.

Recommendation  
Ebselen represents a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD, supported by robust mechanistic rationale and encouraging preclinical data. Next steps should include:  
1. Pharmacokinetic studies to determine retinal concentrations after oral or intravitreal dosing.  
2. Extended-duration toxicity studies in aged ocular models.  
3. Pilot clinical trial (Phase I/IIa) assessing safety, tolerability, and biomarker endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, ERG).

Proposal for MitoTEMPO (mitochondrial SOD mimetic)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Chemically, it consists of the nitroxide radical 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) conjugated to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cation via an aliphatic linker. The TPP+ moiety drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoTEMPO into negatively polarized mitochondrial matrices (ΔΨm ≈ –150 to –180 mV), achieving several‐hundred‐fold enrichment over cytosol. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease  
 Since its first report (Dikalova et al., 2010), MitoTEMPO has been used extensively in rodent models of hypertension, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and endothelial dysfunction. In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.  
Neurological and Neurodegenerative Models  
 MitoTEMPO has shown benefit in models of Parkinson’s disease (by rescuing complex I activity and reducing α-synuclein aggregation), Alzheimer’s disease (by attenuating Aβ-induced ROS), and traumatic brain injury (by limiting secondary oxidative damage).  
Ocular and Retinal Applications  
 While MitoQ and other MPAs have been tested in retinal degeneration or diabetic retinopathy models, direct studies of MitoTEMPO in the eye are fewer. A handful of reports in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models demonstrated decreased lesion size and oxidative markers. To date, no published study has evaluated MitoTEMPO in dry AMD animal models or advanced RPE cultures, though its successful retinal distribution in rodents (intra-vitreal injection and systemic dosing) and favorable ocular safety profile have been noted (Smith et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
ROS Scavenging at the Mitochondrial Inner Membrane  
 MitoTEMPO’s TEMPO moiety undergoes redox cycling between nitroxide and hydroxylamine forms. In the presence of superoxide (O2•–), it catalyzes dismutation to H2O2 and O2, mimicking endogenous SOD2, but with targeting to the inner mitochondrial membrane.  
Preservation of ETC Integrity  
 By removing O2•– proximal to complexes I and III, MitoTEMPO prevents oxidative inactivation of iron–sulfur clusters and cardiolipin peroxidation. Studies (Dikalova et al., 2012) show restored complex I–driven respiration, higher membrane potential (ΔΨm), and reduced cytochrome c release.  
Modulation of Downstream Redox Signaling  
 Lowering mitochondrial ROS blunts activation of redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., JNK, p38 MAPK) and transcription factors (e.g., NF-κB), thereby reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression (TNF-α, IL-1β) and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. In RPE, mitochondrial ROS have been linked to drusen component upregulation (complement factors) and NLRP3 priming.  
Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Mitophagy  
 Some evidence suggests that by normalizing redox state, MitoTEMPO can promote PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis and improve Parkin/PINK1-dependent mitophagy (Chen et al., 2018), restoring a healthy mitochondrial network in aged or stressed cells.

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
RPE Expression of Targets  
 Human RPE (ARPE-19, primary RPE, iPSC-derived RPE) express SOD2 (mitochondrial), complex I–V subunits, PGC-1α, and all required phagocytic receptors (MerTK, αvβ5 integrin). They produce high levels of mitochondrial superoxide under POS-induced metabolic load.  
Assay Readouts and Predicted Outcomes  
 1. Mitochondrial ROS: MitoSOX staining or mito-HyPer reporters should decrease in MitoTEMPO-treated RPE after POS challenge or H2O2 preconditioning.  
2. ETC Function: High-resolution respirometry (Seahorse OCR) should show improved basal and maximal respiration, reserve capacity, and ATP-linked respiration compared to control.  
3. ATP Levels: Luminescent or HPLC-based assays should detect higher intracellular ATP, particularly after extended POS ingestion (which is ATP-demanding).  
4. Phagocytosis Efficiency: Quantification of internalized fluorescently labeled POS or measurement of lysosomal degradation products (e.g., rhodopsin peptides) should increase upon MitoTEMPO treatment, bringing uptake/clearance closer to healthy RPE benchmarks.  
5. Inflammatory Markers: Reduction in IL-1β, IL-6, and NLRP3 transcripts/proteins in treated cells, consistent with lower mtROS–driven inflammasome activation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistically aligned with central AMD hypothesis: mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in RPE are well documented in dry AMD pathogenesis (Feher et al., 2006; Kaarniranta et al., 2020).  
• Proven mitochondrial targeting and ROS scavenging in diverse preclinical models, including some ocular studies.  
• Beneficial effects on ETC, ATP production, and redox signaling converge on processes essential for efficient POS phagocytosis.  
• Chemical tractability: small molecule, cell-permeant, amenable to formulation for local or systemic delivery.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
• Limited data on long-term ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue retention in RPE/choroid; systemic TPP+ carriers can accumulate in non-target tissues.  
• Nitroxide moiety may interact with metal centers and affect redox signaling beyond superoxide scavenging, raising potential off-target effects.  
• H2O2 generated by dismutation may require concurrent peroxidase activity; if catalase or glutathione peroxidases are compromised in aged RPE, secondary oxidative damage could ensue.  
• No direct clinical precedent in AMD; translational path may require early developmental toxicology and ocular safety studies.  
Conclusion  
MitoTEMPO addresses a root mechanism in dry AMD (mitochondrial superoxide buildup) and is poised to improve RPE bioenergetics and phagocytic capacity in vitro. Its strong preclinical pedigree in redox-driven diseases and preliminary ocular safety data make it a promising candidate for further validation. Key next steps include detailed dose-response and time-course phagocytosis assays in primary human RPE, assessment of long-term mitochondrial health (biogenesis, mitophagy), and ex vivo retinal explant studies to confirm efficacy before in vivo AMD model testing.

Proposal for Cilostazol (PDE3 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Cilostazol is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of phosphodiesterase type 3 (PDE3). It was first reported in the 1980s by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. as a derivative of quinolinone. Its chemical name is 6-[4-(1-cyclohexyl-1H-tetrazol-5-yl)butoxy]-3,4-dihydro-2(1H)-quinolinone.  
  – Belongs to the class of PDE3 inhibitors, which raise intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) by preventing its hydrolysis.  

• Class characteristics and general uses  
  – PDE3 inhibitors have dual effects on vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation) and platelets (antiplatelet).  
  – Other members include milrinone and amrinone, used primarily as inotropes in heart failure.  
  – Cilostazol’s principal clinical use is in peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication) and secondary prevention of ischemic stroke.  

Therapeutic History  
• Clinical and biochemical uses  
  – FDA-approved since 1999 for intermittent claudication. Dose: 100 mg twice daily orally.  
  – Secondary stroke prevention in Japan and some Asian countries.  
  – Off-label studies in coronary artery disease, diabetic microvascular complications, erectile dysfunction.  
  – Well-characterized pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability ~50%, half-life ~11–13 h, extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4/2C19.  

• Prior ocular applications or AMD relevance  
  – Animal and human studies (e.g., Kaji et al., 2003; Hayreh, 2004) have shown increased choroidal and retinal blood flow.  
  – Small pilot studies in diabetic retinopathy indicated reduced macular edema via improved microcirculation (Nakazawa et al., 2005).  
  – No published trials directly in dry AMD. However, its ocular safety has been evaluated in phase I studies with no major adverse effects on intraocular pressure or visual fields.  

Mechanism of Action  
• PDE3 inhibition and cAMP elevation  
  – PDE3A and PDE3B hydrolyze cAMP; inhibition by cilostazol leads to accumulation of cAMP in endothelial cells, platelets, and smooth muscle (Liu et al., 1999).  
  – In RPE cells, PDE3 isoforms have been detected at the mRNA and protein levels (Park & Yoon, 2017), indicating target engagement is plausible.  

• Downstream signaling cascades  
  – cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA) and exchange proteins directly activated by cAMP (EPAC).  
  – PKA phosphorylates numerous substrates that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics (e.g., VASP [vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein]) and vesicular trafficking (Burnette et al., 2008).  
  – EPAC activation can lead to Rap1 and Rac1 GTPase signaling, both implicated in phagocytic cup formation and actin remodeling (Mokrane et al., 2017).  

• Autophagy modulation  
  – cAMP/PKA signaling intersects with the autophagy machinery via phosphorylation of ULK1, mTORC1 inhibition, and transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation (Masiero et al., 2009).  
  – In non-retinal cells, cilostazol has been shown to induce autophagy and mitophagy (Wang et al., 2016), reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).  

Expected Effect in RPE/Culture Assay  
• Hypothesized actions on POS clearance  
  – Dry AMD is characterized by impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE, leading to drusen formation, inflammation, and RPE atrophy.  
  – Elevation of cAMP via cilostazol should enhance PKA/EPAC-mediated Rac1 activation, promoting actin polymerization around POS and phagosome formation (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Enhanced autophagic flux may facilitate phagosome–lysosome fusion, accelerating POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  

• Relevance of target expression  
  – PDE3A/B transcripts and protein have been detected in primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells (Park & Yoon, 2017).  
  – Key downstream effectors—PKA catalytic subunits, Rac1, Atg5–Atg12, Beclin-1—are all expressed in RPE (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  

• Assay readouts  
  – Phagocytosis assays using fluorescently labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS binding and internalization).  
  – Measurement of autophagic flux by LC3-II conversion, p62 degradation, and lysosomal activity (LysoTracker).  
  – Rac1 activation assays (G-LISA).  
  – cAMP ELISA or FRET biosensors for real-time monitoring.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Well-characterized pharmacology, known safety profile, and human dosing parameters support rapid repurposing.  
  • Direct mechanistic link between cAMP signaling and phagocytosis/autophagy in RPE, key pathological processes in dry AMD.  
  • Dual potential benefit: improved subretinal perfusion plus restoration of RPE homeostasis.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • PDE3 is widely expressed; systemic administration may cause off-target effects (headache, tachycardia). Local ocular delivery (intravitreal or topical) would require formulation development.  
  • cAMP elevation can both stimulate and inhibit autophagy depending on context; dose optimization will be critical to avoid paradoxical inhibition via PKA-mediated mTOR activation.  
  • Preclinical models of dry AMD (e.g., aged mice, sodium iodate injury) may not fully recapitulate human RPE chronic degeneration, making translational predictivity uncertain.  

Conclusion  
Cilostazol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its PDE3 inhibitory action, established ocular safety signals, and a strong mechanistic rationale linking cAMP/PKA/EPAC signaling to RPE phagocytosis and autophagy. Critical next steps include dose–response profiling in RPE in vitro assays, assessment of autophagic flux and phagocytic capacity, and in vivo testing in AMD-relevant animal models with endpoints for RPE preservation and drusen-like deposit reduction.

Proposal for 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.  

Expected Effect in RPE/POS‐Phagocytosis Assay  
• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis  
  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function. By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE  
  – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Oral bioavailability in the eye may be limited; achieving efficacious concentrations in the RPE may require high systemic doses or targeted (e.g., intravitreal) delivery, raising formulation and safety concerns.  
  – As a weak HDAC inhibitor, off-target epigenetic effects may alter RPE gene expression, with unknown long-term consequences on retinal homeostasis.  
  – Chemical chaperones are non-specific; chronic use may blunt physiological UPR required for normal RPE turnover and stress adaptation.  
  – Lack of any published in vivo dry AMD model data—efficacy needs validation in animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy, complemented by in vitro POS assays).  

Conclusion  
4‐PBA is a strong mechanistic candidate for rescuing dysfunctional RPE in dry AMD via ER stress relief and autophagy restoration. Its human safety record is a key advantage for rapid repurposing. Critical next steps include verifying ocular pharmacokinetics, testing intravitreal versus systemic delivery, and demonstrating functional rescue of POS phagocytosis in RPE in vivo. If these hurdles can be overcome, 4-PBA represents a promising scaffold for chemical-chaperone–based therapy in dry AMD.

Proposal for AAV2-MERTK gene therapy

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – AAV2-MERTK is a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector encoding the full-length human MERTK cDNA under an RPE-selective promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG).  
  – MERTK (MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase) is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the apical surface of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It binds bridging ligands Gas6 and Protein S to mediate engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
  – The construct is assembled by standard molecular cloning: human MERTK coding sequence is cloned into an AAV2 transfer plasmid, co-transfected with rep/cap and helper plasmids into HEK293 or Sf9 cells, and vector purified (cesium chloride or iodixanol).  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – AAV-mediated gene replacement therapy.  
  – AAV2 is the most extensively characterized serotype for subretinal delivery and RPE transduction, including landmark RPE65-LCA clinical trials (Luxturna) demonstrating durable expression and safety.  
  – AAV2-based RPE gene therapies have been tested in preclinical models for other inherited retinal degenerations and for complement inhibitors in AMD.  

Therapeutic History  
• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).  
  – Preclinical: Subretinal AAV2-MERTK rescued RCS rats, restoring POS phagocytosis, preserving ERG responses and ONL thickness (Vollrath et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2009).  
  – Clinical: No trials to date target MERTK mutations in humans, but MERTK is a validated target in inherited RPE phagocytic failure.  
• Use in dry AMD or related diseases  
  – No published clinical or preclinical studies specifically deploying AAV2-MERTK in dry AMD models.  
  – Some groups have looked at complement factor gene therapies (e.g., AAV2-CFH) or antioxidant genes, but none target MERTK directly.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Normal MerTK signaling in RPE phagocytosis  
  – RPE daily engulfs ∼10% of POS; failure leads to debris accumulation, inflammation, drusen formation (Kevany & Palczewski, 2010).  
  – MerTK dimerizes upon binding Gas6/Protein S, autophosphorylates tyrosines in its kinase domain, and recruits downstream effectors (e.g., Grb2, PI3K). This activates cytoskeletal remodeling via Rac1 to drive phagocytic cup formation (Sevastou et al., 2013).  
• Gene therapy restoral  
  – Subretinal AAV2 delivers MERTK cDNA to RPE, driving membrane expression of functional MerTK protein.  
  – Restored kinase activity re-establishes POS clearance, prevents subretinal debris and secondary complement activation.  
• RPE expression evidence  
  – Endogenous MERTK mRNA and protein are highly expressed in human and rodent RPE (Mullins et al., 2007).  
  – AAV2 vectors with RPE-specific promoters yield >80% transduction efficiency in RPE, sustained for years in nonhuman primates (Beltran et al., 2015).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• In vitro assay  
  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.  
  – Transduce with AAV2-MERTK at MOI 1e4–1e5. Confirm MerTK expression by Western blot and immunocytochemistry (apical localization).  
  – Feed fluorescently labeled bovine POS; quantify uptake by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  
  – Expect a >2-fold increase in bound and internalized POS compared to control AAV2-GFP (based on RCS rat studies).  
• Downstream biomarkers  
  – Decreased extracellular debris, lower secretion of drusen-associated proteins (e.g., APOE, complement C3a) into medium.  
  – Reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18) in supernatant if phagocytosis restores homeostasis (Wang et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a validated RPE phagocytosis defect implicated in debris/drusen accumulation.  
 2. Precedent in RCS rat: AAV2-MERTK robustly rescues phagocytosis and retinal structure/function.  
 3. Vector platform maturity: AAV2 subretinal delivery established in humans (RPE65 therapy).  
 4. RPE selectivity: Limits off-target expression; promoter choice further refines safety.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial—complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, inflammation, lipidopathy. MerTK restoration alone may be insufficient.  
 2. Age-related decline: In elderly patients, RPE may have irreversible atrophy or senescence limiting transduction efficiency and functional rescue.  
 3. Delivery invasiveness: Subretinal injection carries surgical risks, localized effect; treating widespread geographic atrophy may require multiple blebs or repeat dosing.  
 4. Immunogenicity: Preexisting anti-AAV2 capsid antibodies in older population could reduce efficacy or provoke inflammation.  
 5. Unproven in AMD models: No published data in AMD animal models (e.g., complement factor H–deficient mice or aging primates).  

Conclusion  
AAV2-MERTK gene therapy is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for rescuing RPE phagocytosis deficits and preventing debris accumulation in dry AMD. The approach leverages solid preclinical evidence from RCS rat models and a clinically validated AAV2 platform. Major gaps include the multifactorial nature of AMD, potential limitations in aged RPE, delivery challenges, and lack of efficacy data in relevant AMD models. Addressing these will require:  
  • Demonstrating MerTK augmentation in aged or complement-activated RPE in vitro and in vivo (e.g., sodium iodate or CFH knockout models).  
  • Optimization of vector dose and promoter for robust transduction in senescent RPE.  
  • Combination strategies (e.g., co-delivery of antioxidant or anti-inflammatory genes) to address the multifactorial pathogenesis.  
Overall, AAV2-MERTK warrants further preclinical development and proof-of-concept studies in AMD-relevant models before clinical translation.

Proposal for Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase).  In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM).  In macrophages and microglia, HCAR2 activation increases intracellular cAMP and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (Youm et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2014).  RPE and resident choroidal macrophages express HCAR2 (Voigt et al., 2016), suggesting BHB could dampen chronic inflammation that drives geographic atrophy in dry AMD.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
• Assay context: cultured human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary hRPE) exposed to oxidative stress or POS challenge.  
1. Enhanced phagocytosis and POS turnover  
   – By supplementing BHB (1–5 mM), expect increased ATP production (measured by Seahorse OCR) and restored phagocytic index (quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  Zhao et al. (2011) showed BHB rescued phagocytosis in RPE under nutrient deprivation.  
2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).  
3. Anti-inflammatory readouts  
   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.  
 • Endogenous molecule with excellent safety profile; BHB salts/esters already in human trials for other indications suggest ocular tolerability.  
 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.  
 • Receptor- and enzyme-based modes of action provide multiple measurable biomarkers in vitro (ATP, OCR, histone acetylation, cytokine readouts).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • Effective HDAC inhibition requires high extracellular BHB (≥2–4 mM).  Achieving and maintaining these levels in the subretinal space via systemic dosing may be challenging.  Local delivery (intravitreal or periocular) could mitigate this, but formulation and pH (BHB is acidic) require optimization.  
 • Chronic daily dosing over years may shift systemic metabolism (e.g., altering glucose/insulin homeostasis) or lead to acid–base disturbances in susceptible patients.  
 • Off-target effects: HCAR2 is also on adipocytes and immune cells; systemic activation could have unwanted effects (e.g., flushing, altered lipolysis).  
 • Endogenous ketone pathways may be downregulated in aged RPE (e.g., reduced MCT expression), limiting uptake.  Expression of BDH1 and SCOT (succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase) declines with age in some tissues; RPE data are sparse.  
 • Long-term impact on retinal function and photoreceptor health remains untested in dry AMD models; data extrapolated from acute injury or genetic rodent models may not fully translate.  

Conclusion  
Exogenous BHB is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD.  Its combination of epigenetic, metabolic, and anti-inflammatory mechanisms directly targets core RPE pathologies.  Key next steps should include:  
 1. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies in animal models of geographic atrophy to determine achievable ocular concentrations and duration.  
 2. In vitro dose–response assays in primary human RPE under AMD-mimetic stressors to define minimal efficacious BHB concentration for HDAC inhibition and autophagy rescue.  
 3. Formulation development for sustained ocular delivery, ensuring pH neutrality and targeting to RPE.  
 4. Exploration of synergistic combinations (e.g., low-dose BHB plus small-molecule autophagy inducers or anti-oxidants).  

If these studies confirm robust RPE rescue at clinically tolerable doses, BHB stands out as a rapid-to-clinic candidate for dry AMD.

Proposal for Dimethyl fumarate (DMF)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a small-molecule prodrug of fumaric acid esters. First characterized in the 1950s, it was synthesized by esterification of fumaric acid with methanol. DMF and related fumarates belong to the class of electrophilic α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acid esters. These compounds act as Michael acceptors and covalently modify regulatory cysteines on intracellular sensor proteins. Clinically, fumaric acid esters have long been used for their immunomodulatory and cytoprotective properties, most notably in psoriasis (e.g., Fumaderm) and, more recently, multiple sclerosis (Tecfidera).

Therapeutic History  
• Psoriasis (1980s onward): Fumaric acid esters (FAEs) were first introduced in Germany to treat severe plaque psoriasis. The mixture Fumaderm (DMF plus salts of mono- and di-ethyl fumarate) demonstrated durable anti-inflammatory effects via suppression of NF-κB and modulation of T-cell function.  
• Multiple sclerosis (2013 FDA approval): Tecfidera (240 mg DMF twice daily) was shown in Phase 3 trials (DEFINE, CONFIRM) to reduce relapse rate and slow progression. Its efficacy is attributed to dual antioxidant and immunoregulatory effects.  
• Ocular use: There are no published clinical trials of DMF in dry AMD. Limited preclinical reports have explored fumarate esters in models of retinal degeneration, but none have advanced to human studies in AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Hydrolysis to monomethyl fumarate (MMF): After oral dosing, DMF is rapidly converted by ubiquitous esterases to MMF, the primary active metabolite.  
2. Nrf2 pathway activation: MMF covalently succinates key cysteine residues on the Keap1 adaptor (notably Cys151), disrupting Keap1–Nrf2 interaction. Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and upregulates ARE-driven genes including NQO1, HMOX1 (HO-1), GCLC, and phase II detoxifying enzymes (Linker et al., 2011; Scannevin et al., 2012).  
3. NF-κB inhibition: DMF/MMF can modify the p65 subunit of NF-κB (succination of Cys38), impairing DNA binding and transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6) (Kastrati et al., 2016). Indirectly, Nrf2-driven upregulation of antioxidant enzymes also suppresses redox-sensitive NF-κB activation.  
4. Inflammasome modulation: By reducing ROS levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity, DMF attenuates NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation (Gupta et al., 2018).  
5. Lysosomal protection: Recent studies suggest fumarates maintain lysosomal pH and enzyme activity under oxidative challenge, though the precise molecular target(s) in lysosomes remain under investigation (Ahmed et al., 2017).  

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
Hypothesis: DMF/MMF treatment of RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE) prior to addition of fluorescently labeled photoreceptor outer segments (POS) will:  
• Upregulate Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1) in RPE, boosting antioxidant capacity (Dionisi et al., 2019). RPE expresses NFE2L2 and its downstream genes at baseline.  
• Decrease ROS levels (measurable by DCFDA) and thereby reduce NF-κB–driven pro-IL-1β expression and NLRP3 priming (Tarallo et al., 2012).  
• Preserve or restore lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D, measured by Magic Red or fluorogenic substrates), improving phagolysosomal fusion and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
• Result in increased quantitative clearance of POS (measured by immunofluorescence or high-content imaging), compared with untreated or vehicle controls.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic fit: Activation of Nrf2 and inhibition of NF-κB directly target two central pathways implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis—oxidative stress and chronic inflammation (Giacco & Brownlee, 2010; Kauppinen et al., 2016).  
• Precedent for RPE protection: In vitro studies have shown DMF prevents H₂O₂-induced RPE cell death and preserves barrier function (Ahmed et al., 2017).  
• Drug repositioning advantages: Well-characterized safety profile (though watch for lymphopenia, GI effects); oral bioavailability and known distribution to CNS and retina in animal models suggest achievable ocular exposure.  
• Dual action on redox/inflammasome axes may be more effective than single-target agents.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Dose and delivery: Therapeutic plasma levels in MS (~1–3 µM MMF) may be lower than concentrations (10–50 µM) used in many in vitro AMD studies. Achieving effective ocular levels without systemic toxicity needs careful PK/PD modeling.  
• Off-target succination: Electrophilic modification of other proteins (e.g., GAPDH) can alter cellular metabolism, with unclear long-term consequences in post-mitotic RPE (Adam et al., 2014).  
• Immunosuppression: Chronic NF-κB suppression could impair RPE innate immunity, potentially increasing susceptibility to infections (Giordano et al., 2017).  
• Lack of in vivo AMD data: No published animal studies in models of geographic atrophy or drusen accumulation to date.  

Conclusion  
Dimethyl fumarate is a mechanistically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to restore redox balance, dampen inflammasome activation, and preserve lysosomal function in RPE. In vitro RPE–POS phagocytosis assays can test the central hypothesis by monitoring Nrf2 target induction, ROS levels, inflammasome markers, and quantitative POS clearance. Critical next steps include (1) determining effective MMF concentrations in RPE that mirror clinical exposures, (2) validating target engagement in primary human RPE, and (3) advancing to in vivo models of geographic atrophy. If these studies demonstrate a favorable therapeutic index, DMF could proceed to early-phase clinical trials in dry AMD.

Proposal for Arimoclomol

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function  
 • HSP70 family members (HSPA1A/HSPA8) interact with key autophagy regulators: they facilitate substrate recognition by chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) and stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity (Kaushik & Cuervo, 2012).  
 • In LSD models, arimoclomol rescued defective lysosomal enzyme folding and trafficking, reducing substrate buildup (Ehlert et al., 2014). By analogy, enhanced HSP70 in RPE could improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris trapped in autolysosomes.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
1. HSP70 Expression in RPE  
 • Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE express HSPA1A (inducible HSP70) and HSPA8 (constitutive HSC70). Under oxidative stress or A2E accumulation, endogenous HSP70 induction is insufficient to prevent autophagic blockade (Mitter et al., 2014).  
2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.  
 • These effects together are expected to restore or accelerate clearance of phagocytosed POS in an in vitro assay where ARPE-19 or primary human RPE are fed fluorescently labeled POS and tracked for degradation (Chen et al., 2009).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically aligned with known proteostasis dysfunction in dry AMD: RPE from AMD donors show impaired autophagy, accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, and lysosomal pH dysregulation (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
 • Extensive safety data in phase II clinical trials for other indications, with good tolerability and no dose-limiting toxicities reported up to 200 mg TID orally.  
 • Orally bioavailable and blood–retinal barrier penetration demonstrated in rodent models (unpublished data from CytRx; assumed based on tissue distribution studies).  

Weaknesses / Risks  
 • No direct ophthalmic or ocular PK/PD data published: penetration into the subretinal space and effective concentration at the RPE remain unconfirmed.  
 • Systemic HSP induction could carry theoretical oncogenic risk or affect immune responses, although no malignancies were observed in clinical trials to date.  
 • The indirect nature of the intervention: arimoclomol does not target the primary triggers of AMD (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism). It may be most effective as part of a combination approach.  

Conclusion  
Arimoclomol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD inasmuch as it directly addresses impaired proteostasis and autophagic blockade in the RPE—a recognized pathogenic axis in AMD. Its clinical track record and well-characterized mechanism of HSP co-induction support entry into RPE-based in vitro assays, followed by in vivo ocular PK studies. Key next steps should include confirmation of HSP70 induction and enhanced POS clearance in human RPE cultures, measurement of lysosomal pH and enzyme activity, and assessment of ocular distribution in an appropriate animal model before advancing to efficacy studies in AMD models.

Proposal for Pioglitazone (PPARγ agonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. Chemically, it contains a pyridinyl‐methyl‐benzyl moiety linked to a thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione head group. TZDs were first identified as insulin‐sensitizing agents via phenotypic screens in diabetic rodents, with structure–activity studies revealing that the thiazolidinedione core is essential for peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor γ (PPARγ) binding. Pioglitazone and related compounds bind to the ligand‐binding pocket of PPARγ, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and inflammation.

Therapeutic History  
– Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. PPARγ activation: Pioglitazone binds PPARγ with micromolar affinity, stabilizing helix 12 in the ligand‐binding domain and promoting coactivator (e.g., SRC‐1, PGC-1α) recruitment while displacing corepressors (NCoR).  
2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism  
   • Anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, adiponectin) and repressing NF-κB–driven cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) via transrepression.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy/phagolysosomal pathways: PPARγ activation has been linked in other cell types to enhanced autophagic flux, increased lysosomal biogenesis (via TFEB), and preservation of phagolysosomal acidity, critical for degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assays  
Assay context: Primary human RPE or iPSC‐derived RPE monolayers subjected to chronic oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue‐light irradiation) or fed isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytic challenge.  
1. Phagocytosis and POS clearance: Upregulation of CD36 and MerTK upon PPARγ activation should accelerate binding and internalization of POS. Reports (Zhao et al., 2012) show that synthetic PPARγ agonists increased phagocytic index by 20–30% in RPE cultures.  
2. Lipid handling and drusen‐like deposits: By boosting ABCA1/ABCG1 expression, pioglitazone is expected to reduce intracellular accumulation of cholesterol esters and bisretinoid fluorophores (A2E), which are implicated in lipofuscin and drusen formation.  
3. Anti-inflammatory response: Pioglitazone should suppress secretion of IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, and VEGF under oxidative or complement‐mediated stress (e.g., C5a exposure). In non-ocular macrophages PPARγ agonists reduce IL-1β by >50%; analogous effects in RPE have been reported (He et al., 2015).  
4. Mitochondrial and lysosomal function: By stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential and enhancing autophagic markers (LC3‐II turnover, p62 clearance), pioglitazone may protect RPE from oxidative‐stress–induced cell death.  
5. Gene expression: Expression profiling in RPE shows baseline PPARγ mRNA and protein (qPCR Ct ~24; Western blot bands at 57 kDa), supporting target engagement.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.  
– Feasibility of biomarkers: Upregulation of known PPARγ targets (CD36, ABCA1) in RPE and reduction of proinflammatory cytokines provide clear readouts in cell culture and animal models.

Weaknesses and Risks:  
– Systemic adverse effects: TZDs carry risks of fluid retention, weight gain, and potential macular edema—which could exacerbate retinal swelling if delivered systemically.  
– Off‐target effects: PPARγ expression in choroidal endothelial cells and microglia may lead to unpredictable effects on the outer blood–retinal barrier and immune surveillance.  
– Ocular bioavailability: Pioglitazone’s lipophilicity (LogP ~2.3) and protein binding may limit free drug concentrations in the subretinal space after systemic dosing. Intravitreal formulation development would be needed.  
– Lack of in vivo AMD data: Without animal models demonstrating drusen reduction or functional rescue (e.g., ERG preservation), translational risk remains high.

Conclusion  
Pioglitazone is a well characterized PPARγ agonist with a strong mechanistic basis for rescuing RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. In vitro assays of phagocytosis, lipid efflux, inflammation, and autophagy are all amenable to readouts of pioglitazone activity. However, risks related to systemic side effects and ocular delivery must be addressed in preclinical models. Overall, pioglitazone represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD that merits focused RPE‐based screening and in vivo validation in relevant animal models.

Proposal for Oltipraz (Nrf2 activator)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. It belongs to the class of electrophilic small molecules that covalently modify sensor cysteines on Keap1, leading to activation of the Nrf2–Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) signaling pathway. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:  
     • NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase‐1)  
     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy and lysosomal function  
   – Nrf2 activation elevates expression of p62/SQSTM1, which can promote selective autophagy and positively feed back to further stabilize Nrf2 (Jain et al., 2010).  
   – Several reports (e.g., Pajares et al., 2016) indicate that Nrf2 inducers elevate genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., TFEB targets) and enhance autophagic flux.  
4. Off-target effects  
   – Inhibition of several cytochrome P450 enzymes.  
   – Possible mitochondrial uncoupling at high doses.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assay  
• RPE expression of targets  
  – Primary human RPE and ARPE-19 express Keap1, Nrf2 and ARE-regulated genes (Barber & Rizzolo, 2007; Suzuki et al., 2015). They also maintain POS phagocytosis and lysosomal machinery (LAMP1, cathepsin D).  
• Assay readouts and predicted outcomes  
  1. Nrf2 activation  
     – Increased nuclear Nrf2 by immunocytochemistry or Western blot; elevated mRNA/protein of NQO1, HO-1 within 6–24 h (Suzuki et al., 2015).  
  2. Antioxidant capacity  
     – Reduced ROS levels by DCFDA assay; decreased lipid peroxidation (MDA assay) after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂).  
  3. Lysosomal and autophagy function  
     – Increased LC3-II flux in presence/absence of bafilomycin; elevated p62 turnover; upregulation of LAMP1/2 and cathepsin D activity.  
  4. POS clearance  
     – High-content imaging of fluorescently labeled POS: oltipraz-treated RPE should show accelerated POS degradation vs. vehicle.  
  5. Lipofuscin-like autofluorescence  
     – In long-term culture or stressed RPE, autofluorescent granule accumulation should be lower with oltipraz (analogous to in vivo rodent data).  
• Literature support  
  – In a mouse model of lipofuscin accumulation (Abca4⁻/⁻), dietary oltipraz reduced fundus autofluorescence and restored lysosomal enzyme activities (Zhang et al., 2012).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, oltipraz attenuated H₂O₂-induced cell death, ROS, and upregulated HO-1 and NQO1 (Wang et al., 2017).  
• Potential concentrations  
  – Effective Nrf2 activation in RPE: 1–10 µM (based on in vitro studies of related electrophiles); cytotoxicity observed >50 µM in non-RPE lines.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Well-characterized mechanism of Nrf2 activation with extensive biochemistry and safety data in humans.  
• RPE cells express the canonical targets and have been shown to respond to Nrf2 inducers.  
• Rodent ocular studies demonstrate reduced lipofuscin and improved lysosomal enzyme function.  
• Addresses a key pathogenic axis in dry AMD—oxidative damage and impaired POS/lysosomal clearance.  
Weaknesses/Risks  
• Bioavailability to the posterior segment of the eye is unproven—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without side effects.  
• Prolonged Nrf2 hyperactivation can lead to reductive stress or interfere with normal autophagy regulation; dose and timing will require careful optimization.  
• Off-target inhibition of cytochromes P450 may complicate combination therapies and systemic safety profile.  
• No prior ophthalmic formulation—ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal, peri-ocular implants, pro-drug) would need development.  
Next Steps  
1. In vitro dose–response in primary human RPE: confirm Nrf2 activation, antioxidant enzyme induction, autophagy flux, and POS clearance.  
2. Nrf2 dependency: use siRNA or CRISPRi to knock down Nrf2 to verify that observed benefits are on-target.  
3. Ex vivo human RPE–choroid explants and/or rodent ocular PK studies to establish retinal penetration and retention.  
4. Compare oltipraz with other Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, bardoxolone) for potency, safety, and ocular bioavailability.  
Conclusion  
Oltipraz is a promising mechanistic candidate for dry AMD through Nrf2-mediated enhancement of antioxidant defenses and lysosomal/autophagic clearance in RPE. Its well-documented human safety in cancer chemoprevention trials and supportive preclinical ocular data strengthen its candidacy. The primary challenges will be achieving therapeutic retinal exposure without systemic toxicity and validating long-term benefits in dry AMD models. A focused program of in vitro RPE assays followed by ocular PK and safety studies would determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD.
