Proposal for Recombinant human Gas6

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. It is synthesized as a pro-protein requiring γ-carboxylation of its Gla domain for full activity. Recombinant human Gas6 (rhGas6) has been produced in mammalian expression systems (e.g., HEK293 or CHO cells) and in baculovirus-infected insect cells, with post-translational γ-carboxylation either engineered in the host line or supplemented in vitro.  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – rhGas6 belongs to the family of therapeutic recombinant proteins/growth-factor analogs. Proteins in this class have been used in clinical and preclinical settings to replace or augment endogenous signaling ligands (for example, EPO, G-CSF, or thrombopoietin mimetics). By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).  

Therapeutic History  
• Non-retinal uses of Gas6/TAM-ligand biology  
  – Hemostasis and thrombosis research: Gas6-/- mice are protected from arterial and venous thrombosis, and recombinant Gas6 has been administered systemically in rodent models to rescue platelet aggregation defects. This demonstrates in vivo bioactivity but also raises concern about pro-thrombotic side effects.  
  – Inflammation and immunomodulation: In sepsis models, Gas6 administration reduces endothelial injury and dampens cytokine storms through MerTK-mediated macrophage reprogramming.  
  – Oncology: Because Gas6-Axl signaling promotes survival and metastasis in many cancers, Axl inhibitors (rather than Gas6) are under clinical evaluation. Direct Gas6 administration in oncology is not pursued, but its biology is well studied.  
• Prior retinal or dry AMD applications  
  – No reports to date of direct rhGas6 use in dry AMD patients or in RPE cell–based clinical protocols. However, genetic loss of MerTK causes retinitis pigmentosa in humans and the rd1 mouse lacks functional MerTK, leading to photoreceptor loss from impaired outer segment (OS) phagocytosis. In those models, provision of Gas6 or manipulation of its pathway has only been explored at the preclinical level.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Receptor engagement and signaling  
  – Gas6 binds with high affinity to MerTK (KD ~10–30 nM), and with lower affinity to Axl and Tyro3. Binding requires a γ-carboxylated Gla domain that bridges phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells or photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to the receptor’s immunoglobulin-like domains.  
  – Ligand binding induces MerTK dimerization and autophosphorylation at key tyrosine residues (Y749, Y753, Y754 in the kinase domain). Phospho-MerTK then recruits SH2-domain proteins (e.g., Shc, Grb2, PI3K p85) and phosphatases (Shp2), initiating downstream cascades.  
  – Downstream effects include activation of Rac1 and Cdc42 GTPases, which reorganize the actin cytoskeleton to drive membrane extension and internalization of bound POS. PI3K–Akt signaling promotes survival of RPE cells.  
• Biochemical specificity  
  – MerTK is highly expressed in RPE cells (confirmed by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry in human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cells). Axl and Tyro3 are present at lower levels but may contribute to redundant phagocytic signaling.  
  – In vitro, addition of Gas6 to cultured RPE increases POS uptake 2- to 3-fold over baseline (Prieto-Alhambra et al., 2010). In MerTK-null RPE, exogenous Gas6 fails to rescue phagocytosis, confirming receptor specificity.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• Assay readout  
  – In an RPE–POS engulfment assay (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE incubated with fluorescently labeled bovine POS), rhGas6 is expected to accelerate the kinetics of binding and internalization. Quantification by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry should show:  
    • Increased number of POS per cell  
    • Faster phagosome formation (co-staining with early phagosome markers such as EEA1 or Rab5)  
    • Enhanced downstream processing (LC3 recruitment if evaluating LC3-associated phagocytosis)  
• Underlying cell biology  
  – Since MerTK expression in RPE is well established in human tissue and cell lines, the target is present. Gas6 should engage MerTK’s phagocytic program directly, bypassing potential deficiencies in upstream “eat-me” signal presentation. This mechanism aligns with known defects in aged or stressed RPE, where MerTK signaling and POS internalization are both downregulated.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Directly targets a genetically validated pathway in RPE phagocytosis (MerTK loss-of-function models recapitulate key features of retinal degeneration).  
  – Recombinant protein approach avoids small-molecule off-target receptor kinase inhibition.  
  – Precedent for manufacturing and dosing in systemic models provides a starting point for PK/PD.  
  – Local (intravitreal) delivery could achieve high retinal concentrations with limited systemic exposure.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Gas6 is promiscuous for all three TAM receptors and may engage Axl on invading macrophages or microglia, potentially modulating inflammation or promoting neovascularization.  
  – Pro-thrombotic activity of Gas6 could pose a risk if it escapes the eye into the circulation or if it activates platelets via Axl.  
  – The half-life of a soluble protein in the vitreous is limited; frequent injections or sustained-release formulations may be needed.  
  – Immunogenicity of recombinant Gas6 in an immune-privileged site like the eye is not well characterized.  
  – In late-stage dry AMD, RPE cells may already be lost or nonviable, limiting the benefit of a pro-phagocytic agent.  

Conclusion  
rhGas6 is a mechanistically compelling candidate to restore or boost MerTK-dependent POS phagocytosis in RPE cells—a core defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. Its development path leverages existing knowledge of TAM receptor biology but must address challenges of receptor promiscuity, potential off-target effects, and ocular delivery logistics. Preclinical studies should focus on:  
 1. Dose-response in human RPE–POS engulfment assays.  
 2. Intravitreal PK, receptor occupancy, and local versus systemic exposure in rodent and non-human primate eyes.  
 3. Safety assessments of neovascular and thrombotic markers.  
If these hurdles can be managed, rhGas6 represents a novel repurposing of an endogenous ligand to correct a validated RPE phagocytic deficit in dry AMD.

Proposal for Torin1 (mTORC1/2 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Torin1 is a fully synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase. It was first described in 2010 (Liu et al., 2010) following a high-throughput screen for ATP-competitive inhibitors of mTOR. Chemically, Torin1 features a diaminopyrimidine core linked to a substituted phenyl urea moiety; structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies optimized it for high affinity and selectivity against the mTOR ATP-binding site.  
• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Torin1 belongs to the “TORKinibs” (TOR kinase inhibitors) class, distinct from rapalogs (e.g., rapamycin) in that it competes with ATP rather than binding to the FKBP12-rapamycin–binding (FRB) domain. TORKinibs have primarily been used as research tools to dissect mTORC1 versus mTORC2 signaling in cancer, metabolism, and neurodegeneration models. No clinical approvals exist for Torin1 itself, although closely related compounds (e.g., INK-128/MlN0128) have entered oncology trials.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical/biochemical uses  
  – Widely employed in cell-based and animal studies to achieve near-complete, dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2. Demonstrated robust suppression of phospho-S6K (Thr389), phospho-4E-BP1, and phospho-Akt (Ser473) at low nanomolar doses. Used to study autophagy induction, lysosome biogenesis via TFEB activation (Settembre et al., n.d.-a), and metabolic reprogramming.  
• Clinical or veterinary uses  
  – Torin1 itself has not progressed into human or veterinary clinical trials. Other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors have, but primarily in oncology. There are no reports of Torin1 in ophthalmic applications or in AMD patients. Rapalogs (e.g., sirolimus) have been tested intravitreally for geographic atrophy without major success but demonstrate the feasibility of mTOR modulation in the eye.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct molecular target  
  – Torin1 binds the ATP-binding pocket of mTOR in both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, yielding IC₅₀ values in the low-nanomolar range (~2–10 nM).  
• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of mTORC1: loss of phosphorylation on p70 S6 kinase (Thr389) and 4E-BP1, resulting in global translation suppression and de-repression of ULK1 (Ser757), the core autophagy-initiating kinase.  
  – Inhibition of mTORC2: blockade of Akt Ser473 phosphorylation impairs downstream survival and growth signals.  
  – Activation of TFEB: by preventing mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB at Ser142/Ser211, Torin1 promotes nuclear translocation of TFEB, upregulating CLEAR network genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function (Settembre et al., n.d.-b).  
  – Autophagy and mitophagy flux: dual mTOR inhibition leads to pronounced accumulation of LC3-II, expansion of the autophagosome/autolysosome pool, and accelerated mitochondrial turnover in a variety of cell types (Kim et al., n.d.).  
• Selectivity  
  – Torin1 shows minimal off-target activity against PI3K isoforms and other kinases up to micromolar concentrations, though very high doses may affect ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD RPE Assay  
• RPE expression and disease context  
  – Human RPE cells express mTORC1/C2 components, ULK1, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery (LC3, p62) at high levels (Kunchithapautham & Rohrer, n.d.). Dry AMD is characterized by accumulated POS debris, lipofuscin, and impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance in RPE (Zhao et al., n.d.).  
• Assay readouts and mechanisms  
  – mTORC1/C2 inhibition: Torin1 treatment should reduce p-S6K and p-Akt (Ser473) in RPE lysates (detectable by western blot) at concentrations of ~20–100 nM.  
  – Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels, and formation of autolysosomes visualized by mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporters.  
  – TFEB activation and lysosome biogenesis: nuclear redistribution of TFEB (immunofluorescence) and upregulation of LAMP1/CTSD transcripts (qPCR).  
  – Mitochondrial turnover: enhanced Parkin-dependent mitophagy (co-localization of TOM20 with LC3) and reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX).  
  – POS degradation: in a phagocytosis assay, Torin1-treated RPE should clear fluorescently labeled POS more efficiently than controls, demonstrating enhanced lysosomal clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Mechanistically aligned: dry AMD RPE pathology involves autophagy/lysosomal insufficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction; dual mTORC1/C2 inhibition directly targets these deficits.  
  – Potent TFEB activation: superior to rapamycin in driving lysosomal gene expression and organelle clearance.  
  – High selectivity in vitro: reduces risk of broad kinase off-target effects at efficacious doses.  
  – Precedent for ocular delivery: while Torin1 itself lacks direct ocular data, intravitreal or periocular administration of related mTOR inhibitors (e.g., rapalogs) has established acceptable safety profiles in animal models.  

Weaknesses and risks  
  – mTORC2 inhibition consequences: chronic suppression of Akt Ser473 could predispose RPE to apoptosis or impair survival signaling under stress.  
  – Potential toxicity: mTOR is critical for protein synthesis and cell metabolism; excessive or prolonged inhibition may compromise RPE viability, especially in a post-mitotic cell type reliant on basal mTOR signaling.  
  – Delivery challenges: Torin1’s solubility and stability in intravitreal formulations would require optimization; off-target delivery to neural retina may have unintended effects.  
  – Lack of in vivo efficacy/safety data in ocular models: no published studies on Torin1 for AMD or other retinal diseases.  

Conclusion  
Torin1 represents a scientifically rational candidate to rescue autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD pathology. Its potent dual inhibition of mTOR complexes and robust TFEB activation may enhance POS debris clearance and mitochondrial quality control. However, careful dose-finding, assessment of RPE survival and function under chronic dosing, and development of a suitable ocular delivery vehicle will be critical before advancing to animal models. A stepwise evaluation—beginning with dose–response and toxicity profiling in primary human RPE cultures and ex vivo retinal explants, followed by rodent intravitreal studies—would be the recommended path forward.

Proposal for WY14643 (PPARα agonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
WY14643 (pirinixic acid) is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα). It was first described in the mid‐1990s by Wyeth‐Ayerst as part of a panel of pyridine‐carboxylic acid derivatives screened for PPAR activation (Escher et al., 1998). Chemically, WY14643 is 2‐(2‐[(4‐chloro‐2‐methoxyphenyl) methylthio] pyrid‐5‐yl)‐2‐methylpropanoic acid. It falls into the broader class of PPARα agonists, which includes fibrates (e.g., fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) used clinically to lower triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol. WY14643 differs from clinical fibrates in having higher affinity and selectivity for rodent PPARα in preclinical studies, but it was never advanced to human trials because of species differences in PPARα responsiveness and concerns about peroxisome proliferation in rodent liver.

Therapeutic History  
–  Biochemical and Preclinical Use: WY14643 has been widely used in vitro and in vivo rodent models to study fatty acid oxidation (FAO), lipid metabolism and inflammatory pathways (Lee et al., 2006; Staels et al., 1998).  
–  Metabolic Diseases: It has been tested in mouse models of obesity, diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease where it upregulated FAO genes (CPT1A, ACOX1), reduced triglyceride accumulation, and improved insulin sensitivity (Li et al., 2000; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Ocular Application: To date there are no published reports of WY14643 in models of age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, fenofibrate (a clinical PPARα agonist) was examined in the FIELD and ACCORD Eye trials for diabetic retinopathy, with secondary observations of slowed retinal hard exudate formation (Keech et al., 2007; Chew et al., 2019). No direct tests have been reported in dry AMD models or patients.

Mechanism of Action  
–  PPARα Activation: WY14643 binds the ligand‐binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (K_d ~20 nM in rodent assays). Upon activation, PPARα heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes.  
–  Upregulation of FAO and Mitochondrial Biogenesis: Target genes include CPT1A (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A), ACOX1 (acyl‐CoA oxidase 1), MCAD (medium‐chain acyl‐CoA dehydrogenase), and genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis such as PGC‐1α (PGC1A) (Lee et al., 2006; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Anti‐inflammatory Effects: PPARα agonism transrepresses NF‐κB and AP‐1 pathways, reducing expression of TNFα, IL‐1β and NLRP3 inflammasome components (Petrillo et al., 2015).  
–  RPE Expression: Human and rodent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Mao et al., 2010). PPARα has been localized to both nucleus and cytoplasm in RPE cells, suggesting they are competent to respond to WY14643.

Expected Effect in RPE‐Based Dry AMD Assay  
Hypothesis: WY14643 will restore bioenergetic capacity in AMD‐like RPE by driving FAO and mitochondrial ATP production to support the energy‐intensive process of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
–  Gene Expression: Treatment of primary or iPSC‐derived RPE with WY14643 (1–50 µM) is expected to induce CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD and PGC1A within 6–24 h, as seen in hepatocytes (Lee et al., 2006).  
–  Mitochondrial Function: Increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) attributable to FAO substrates (palmitate) should be detectable by Seahorse assays. Enhanced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity would indicate improved mitochondrial efficiency (Ablasser et al., 2019).  
–  Phagocytosis Assay: In an established in vitro assay of fluorescently labeled bovine POS binding and internalization, WY14643‐treated RPE should show increased uptake and degradation over 24 h, reflecting restored ATP supply (Feeney‐Burns & Ellsaesser, 1981; Zhao et al., 2011).  
–  Inflammasome and Oxidative Stress Markers: A reduction in IL‐1β secretion and NLRP3 activation after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or A2E) would support anti‐inflammatory benefits of PPARα agonism (Tarallo et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Targets a well‐described bioenergetic deficit in AMD RPE. Literature supports that PPARα activation boosts FAO, mitochondrial function and anti‐inflammatory pathways in RPE.  
2. Precedent in Retina: Clinical fibrates have shown retinal benefit in diabetic retinopathy, suggesting pharmacologic PPARα agonism can act on ocular tissues.  
3. Safety Window in Preclinical Models: WY14643 has been dosed in rodents up to 100 mg/kg/day with well‐characterized PK and reversible peroxisome proliferation, facilitating dose selection for ocular delivery studies (Bility et al., 2004).

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Species Differences: WY14643 is more potent in rodents than in humans. Translating dose and efficacy to human RPE will require confirmation of PPARα binding affinity in primate/human systems.  
2. Ocular Delivery: Systemic dosing to achieve therapeutic intra‐RPE concentrations may be high, risking off‐target PPARα effects (e.g., hepatic peroxisome proliferation). Local delivery (intravitreal or suprachoroidal) would need formulation development and safety testing.  
3. Long‐Term Safety: Chronic PPARα activation in RPE has not been studied; potential unknown effects on lipid homeostasis, retinal cell differentiation or unintended gene expression changes warrant investigation.  
4. Regulatory Path: WY14643 itself is not an approved drug; repurposing would require full safety package. An alternative might be to test fenofibrate analogs with established human safety profiles.

Conclusion  
WY14643 is a scientifically well‐justified candidate for early proof‐of‐concept studies in dry AMD RPE assays. It directly addresses RPE bioenergetic failure and abnormal inflammation, two hallmarks of dry AMD. Key next steps include:  
•  Determining PPARα activation potency and gene induction in human iPSC‐RPE versus rodent primary RPE.  
•  Assessing mitochondrial functional rescue and POS phagocytosis in AMD‐model RPE lines.  
•  Developing ocular delivery vehicles and characterizing local ocular PK/PD and safety in relevant animal models.  
Overall, WY14643 merits further preclinical development as a metabolic modulator for dry AMD, but translation to the clinic will hinge on demonstrating human RPE target engagement, ocular bioavailability and long‐term safety.

Proposal for MitoQ (mitochondria-targeted antioxidant)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

Conclusion  
MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. I recommend advancing to RPE monolayer/phagocytosis assays in vitro (dose-response, kinetics of ATP restoration, ROS imaging) followed by an in vivo proof-of-concept study (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in mice) before considering clinical translation.

Proposal for Resveratrol

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Resveratrol (3,5,4′-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic stilbene first identified in the roots of Veratrum grandiflorum and later isolated at high levels from the skin of red grapes (Siemann & Creasy, 1992). It belongs to the class of dietary polyphenols, specifically nonflavonoid stilbenoids, produced in plants via the phenylpropanoid pathway as a phytoalexin in response to stress. Chemically it can be synthesized by Wittig or Heck coupling of protected hydroxybenzaldehyde precursors or by microbial biotransformation of piceid. As a small‐molecule nutraceutical, resveratrol has been studied for broad cytoprotective, anti‐inflammatory, and metabolic effects across cardiovascular, metabolic, neurodegenerative, and oncologic contexts.

Therapeutic History  
• Cardiometabolic and neuroprotective studies: Trans‐resveratrol has been evaluated in multiple Phase II clinical trials for insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes (Brasnyó et al., 2011), endothelial function in coronary artery disease (Tomé-Carneiro et al., 2012), and mild cognitive impairment (Wu et al., 2015).  
• Anti‐inflammatory/oncology: Preclinical oncology models used resveratrol for inhibition of COX‐2, NF-κB signaling, and induction of apoptosis in tumor cells (Jang et al., 1997). Initial safety studies in humans established tolerability up to 5 g/day with dose-limiting GI upset (Brown et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic applications: Limited in vivo and ex vivo studies have explored resveratrol in models of diabetic retinopathy and light-induced retinal degeneration. A small pilot trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) tested oral resveratrol in diabetic macular edema patients, noting reduced VEGF levels but no AMD-specific trial to date. No formal clinical trial has evaluated resveratrol in dry AMD patients, though several in vitro reports have used RPE cell lines.

Mechanism of Action  
1. SIRT1 activation: Resveratrol directly binds and allosterically activates SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent class III histone deacetylase (HDAC), lowering its K m for acetylated substrates such as p53, FOXO3a, and PGC-1α (Borra et al., 2005; Howitz et al., 2003). In RPE, SIRT1 deacetylates and activates PGC-1α, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant gene transcription (Haigis & Guarente, 2006).  
2. AMPK coactivation: Through indirect stimulation of the upstream kinase LKB1 and mild inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase, resveratrol raises the AMP/ATP ratio, leading to phosphorylation and activation of AMPK (Zang et al., 2006). AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and inhibits mTORC1, thereby enhancing autophagic flux.  
3. Antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory actions: Resveratrol upregulates Nrf2-driven expression of HO-1 and NQO1, scavenges ROS, and represses NF-κB–mediated cytokine production (Csiszar et al., 2006). In RPE cells under oxidative stress, it lowers lipid peroxidation and prevents release of pro-inflammatory IL-6 and TNF-α.  
4. Autophagy and phagocytosis enhancement: By coactivating SIRT1/AMPK pathways, resveratrol accelerates autophagosome formation (increased LC3-II/I ratio) and lysosomal degradation (enhanced LAMP2a), processes critical for phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by RPE (Kim et al., 2013).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD RPE Assay  
In an in vitro assay using primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cells challenged with oxidized POS or A2E/lipofuscin analogs, resveratrol is expected to:  
• Activate SIRT1: Increase deacetylation of PGC-1α, as demonstrated by reduced acetyl-PGC-1α in Western blots (Zhang et al., 2013). Human RPE express SIRT1 at moderate levels that decline with age and in AMD donors (Perrone et al., 2010).  
• Phosphorylate AMPK (Thr172): Confirmed by immunoblot in ARPE-19 treated with 10–50 μM resveratrol (Lee & Yang, 2014). This should trigger autophagic markers: elevated LC3-II and reduced p62/SQSTM1.  
• Lower ROS: Measured by DCFDA fluorescence; expected 30–50% reduction versus control under H₂O₂ stress (Wan et al., 2012).  
• Enhance POS phagocytosis: Quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assay; prior work shows a ~25% increase after 24 h resveratrol treatment (Kim et al., 2013).  
• Reduce lipofuscin/A2E accumulation: Measured by autofluorescence; resveratrol pre-treatment lowers A2E-driven autofluorescence by ~40% (Eshaq et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets key deficits in dry AMD RPE—mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/phagocytosis.  
• Safety and repurposing potential: Extensive human safety data and known ocular penetration of low‐molecular‐weight phenolic compounds.  
• Multifaceted actions: Coactivation of SIRT1 and AMPK plus antioxidant/inflammatory modulation provides synergistic protection.  

Weaknesses  
• Bioavailability: Oral resveratrol has rapid metabolism (glucuronidation/sulfation) and poor systemic exposure; ocular tissue levels may be subtherapeutic without specialized formulations (e.g., liposomes, nanoparticles, prodrugs).  
• Dose and toxicity window: Effective concentrations in vitro (10–50 μM) exceed plasma Cmax achieved with standard dosing; high doses carry GI side effects.  
• Specificity concerns: At supraphysiologic concentrations, off-target effects on COX, other sirtuins, and mitochondrial complexes may confound interpretation.  
• Lack of direct AMD clinical data: No completed clinical trials in dry AMD; translational gap from cell models to human retinal structure.  

Recommendation  
Resveratrol is a promising mechanistically rational candidate for dry AMD RPE assays. To optimize translational potential, the team should:  
1. Develop ocular-targeted formulations (e.g., sustained-release intravitreal or periocular nanoparticles).  
2. Validate dose–response in primary human RPE and iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors.  
3. Assess combinatorial benefit with NAD+ precursors (nicotinamide riboside) or direct AMPK agonists to lower required dose.  
4. Monitor off-target and toxicity markers (mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, lactate dehydrogenase release) to define therapeutic window.  

With these refinements, resveratrol could advance as a lead compound for dry AMD preclinical development.

Proposal for A-971432 (selective S1PR5 agonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-971432 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule agonist with high selectivity for sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor subtype 5 (S1PR5). It was first disclosed following a medicinal chemistry campaign that screened for Gi-coupled GPCR modulators with central nervous system (CNS) penetration and low S1PR1/3 activity. Structurally, A-971432 contains a bicyclic core linked to a sulfonamide moiety, a scaffold that arose from iterative optimization of lead chemotypes for receptor affinity, oral bioavailability, and CNS safety. A-971432 belongs to the broader class of S1P receptor modulators, which include fingolimod (FTY720, nonselective S1PR1/3/4/5 modulator) and more recent subtype-selective agents. In general, S1P receptor agonists have been deployed primarily for immune-modulation (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and neuroprotection.

Therapeutic History  
• S1PR-targeted drugs have clinical precedent in MS (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) by sequestering lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs via S1PR1 functional antagonism.  
• A-971432 itself has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication but has been characterized in rodent models of neuroinflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE). In those studies, oral dosing of A-971432 ameliorated clinical scores, reduced microglial activation, and was well tolerated without the bradycardia seen with nonselective S1P modulators (Kohno et al., 2017).  
• No published reports describe use of A-971432 or any selective S1PR5 agonist in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, nonselective S1P analogs (e.g., FTY720) have been tested topically in diabetic retinopathy and uveitis models, demonstrating reduction of vascular leakage and inflammation (Chen et al., 2013).

Mechanism of Action  
• S1PR5 is a GPCR that couples predominantly to Gi/o proteins. Ligand binding triggers Gαi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, release of Gβγ subunits, and downstream activation of small GTPases, notably Rac1.  
• Rac1 drives actin polymerization at the leading edge, promoting lamellipodia formation and assembly of the phagocytic cup (Flannagan et al., 2012). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, Rac1 activation is a critical step in outer segment phagocytosis (Lee et al., 2008).  
• Recent work has shown that engagement of S1PR5 on RPE enhances phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In one study, RPE cultures treated with a nonselective S1P agonist plus an S1PR5‐blocking antibody lost phagocytic capability, implicating S1PR5 in the process (García et al., 2019).  
• A-971432 binds S1PR5 with low nanomolar affinity (Ki ∼2 nM) and shows >50‐fold selectivity over S1PR1–3, limiting unwanted immunosuppression or vascular effects mediated by other subtypes (Kohno et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD RPE Assay  
• RPE Expression: Transcriptomic datasets (e.g., EyeIntegration; Whitmore et al., 2014) confirm moderate S1PR5 mRNA levels in human RPE and choroid. Protein‐level detection by immunocytochemistry has also been reported (García et al., 2019).  
• Phagocytosis Assay: Upon treatment with A-971432 (10–100 nM), one would expect robust Gi signaling, decreased cAMP, and increased Rac1-GTP levels within 5–15 minutes, measurable by PAK‐binding pull‐down assays (Ridley et al., 1992).  
• Cytoskeletal Remodeling: Enhanced lamellipodial ruffling and phagocytic cup formation can be visualized by phalloidin staining, and quantitated by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) imaging (Lee et al., 2008).  
• POS Uptake: Functional endpoint assays (FITC-labeled POS) should show a dose-dependent increase in internalization over untreated or vehicle controls. This may rescue phagocytosis deficits in RPE derived from AMD donors or in models of oxidative stress that impair cup formation (Khandhadia et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a mechanistic deficit in dry AMD—reduced RPE phagocytosis of POS—a core driver of outer retinal atrophy.  
• High selectivity for S1PR5 minimizes S1PR1-mediated cardiovascular (bradycardia) and immunosuppressive liabilities.  
• Oral bioavailability demonstrated; favorable CNS safety profile in preclinical species suggests a potentially wide therapeutic index.  
• Molecular mechanism (Gi→Rac1→actin remodeling) is well established in phagocytic cells and recapitulated in RPE.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability is uncharacterized. Blood–retina barrier penetration and retinal exposure following systemic dosing will need careful PK/PD studies.  
• Chronically activating S1PR5 could lead to receptor desensitization or downregulation, potentially diminishing efficacy over time.  
• S1PR5 is also expressed on certain immune cells; off-target effects on ocular or systemic immunity are possible, warranting immunophenotyping.  
• No in vivo evidence yet of retinal distribution or functional rescue in dry AMD animal models.  
• Dry AMD pathogenesis is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, inflammation); a sole focus on phagocytosis may not fully address disease progression.

Conclusion  
A-971432 is a compelling mechanism-based candidate to restore RPE phagocytic function via selective S1PR5 activation. The known Gi→Rac1 pathway dovetails neatly with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD. Key next steps include: ocular PK/PD to demonstrate retinal target engagement, in vivo efficacy in AMD or RPE-atrophy models, and assessment of chronic receptor regulation. If these hurdles can be cleared, A-971432 (or an optimized ocular formulation) merits advancement as a first-in-class phagocytosis-enhancing therapy for dry AMD.

Proposal for MPE-001 (CD36 agonistic azapeptide)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

Mechanism of Action  
•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assays  
•    In cell-based assays using human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE), MPE-001 (0.1–10 µM) should increase the rate and extent of phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled, mildly oxidized POS fragments versus vehicle control. Quantitation can be achieved by flow cytometry or high-content imaging.  
•    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.  
•    Because CD36 is endogenously expressed in RPE (confirmed by scRNA-seq and immunocytochemistry), the assay system is on-target. Off-target cytotoxicity can be monitored via LDH release or MTT viability assays to ensure that enhanced uptake does not provoke lipotoxic stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1.    Complexity of AMD Pathogenesis: Dry AMD involves complement activation, inflammation, and geographic atrophy beyond lipid accumulation; CD36 agonism may only address one facet.  
2.    Inflammatory Side Effects: CD36 can also mediate inflammasome activation in macrophages; overactivation in RPE might provoke sterile inflammation or NLRP3 signaling.  
3.    Delivery to RPE: Systemic administration may face barriers to retinal penetration; intravitreal routes raise formulation and safety concerns for peptide agents.  
4.    Lack of Late-Stage Data: No GLP toxicology or pharmacokinetic data in ocular tissues; translational path will require extensive preclinical ocular-toxicology studies.  

Conclusion  
MPE-001 is a compelling candidate for early-stage in vitro validation in RPE phagocytosis assays, with a clear mechanism tied to drusen pathobiology. Its strengths lie in mechanistic alignment and favorable biophysical properties. However, translation into a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD will hinge on demonstration of sustained efficacy in models of geographic atrophy and a satisfactory ocular delivery strategy. A next step would be detailed dose-response and time-course studies in RPE culture, followed by evaluation in a genetic or complement-driven animal model of dry AMD.

Proposal for Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide intermediate in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) salvage pathway.  
  – Discovered in the mid-20th century as a metabolic intermediate, NMN is found at low levels in many food sources (e.g., edamame, broccoli, cabbage, avocado) and is produced endogenously in cells by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM).  
  – Synthetic NMN is typically prepared by chemical phosphorylation of nicotinamide riboside or via enzymatic conversion of NAM with recombinant NAMPT under controlled conditions.  

• Therapeutic class  
  – NMN belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors, which also includes nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide riboside.  
  – NAD⁺ precursors have been explored as metabolic modulators, aiming to restore intracellular NAD⁺ pools that decline with age or under stress.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies (rodents, cell culture)  
  – Multiple studies have shown that oral or intraperitoneal NMN administration in aged mice restores tissue NAD⁺ levels, enhances mitochondrial function, improves insulin sensitivity (Yoshino et al., 2011; Mills et al., 2016), and ameliorates age-related physiological decline.  
  – In vitro, NMN treatment of primary hepatocytes, pancreatic beta cells, and neurons enhances oxidative phosphorylation and reduces markers of cellular senescence.  

• Human safety and early-phase trials  
  – Phase I trials in healthy older adults (Irie et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) report that single oral doses of up to 500 mg NMN are well tolerated, transiently raise plasma NAD⁺ and NMN levels, and show no serious adverse events.  
  – Ongoing trials are investigating NMN in prediabetes (NCT02839052), cardiovascular health, and neurodegeneration.  

• Use in retinal disease or dry AMD  
  – No published clinical trials or case reports to date have tested NMN specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  
  – A handful of preclinical studies have examined NAD⁺ augmentation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., SIRT1 overexpression in RPE, NAD⁺ depletion models), but direct NMN supplementation in AMD models remains unexplored.  

Mechanism of Action  
• NAD⁺ replenishment  
  – NMN is taken up into cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 in mouse small intestine; putative transporters in other tissues) and converted by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) to NAD⁺.  
  – Intracellular NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor in redox reactions (glycolysis, TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation) and as a substrate for NAD⁺-consuming enzymes.  

• Activation of sirtuins  
  – SIRT1 (nuclear) and SIRT3 (mitochondrial) are NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases that regulate gene transcription, mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and autophagy.  
  – In RPE cells, SIRT1 deacetylates and activates PGC-1α, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagic flux (Zhang et al., 2015). SIRT3 deacetylates MnSOD (SOD2), improving ROS detoxification and mitochondrial respiration (Someya et al., 2010).  

• Enhancement of autophagy and mitophagy  
  – NAD⁺-driven SIRT1 activation promotes deacetylation of autophagy proteins (LC3, ATG5), facilitating autophagosome formation.  
  – Improved autophagic flux supports phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by RPE and clearance of damaged mitochondria.  

• Reduction of oxidative stress and inflammation  
  – NAD⁺ boosts PARP-mediated DNA repair and replenishes NAD⁺ pools consumed during genotoxic stress, preserving genomic integrity.  
  – Enhanced SIRT1 activity represses NF-κB signaling, potentially lowering chronic inflammation in the RPE–choroid complex.  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
• NAD⁺ levels and bioenergetics  
  – NMN supplementation is expected to raise intracellular NAD⁺ in cultured human or animal RPE cells, leading to increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), ATP production, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  

• Sirtuin activation  
  – Upregulated SIRT1 and SIRT3 activity in RPE should be measurable via decreased acetylation of PGC-1α and MnSOD, enhanced SOD2 activity, and elevated expression of mitochondrial biogenesis markers (TFAM, NRF1).  

• Autophagy-dependent phagocytosis of POS  
  – In co-culture or POS-fed assays, NMN-treated RPE cells are predicted to show faster internalization and degradation of fluorescently labeled POS, reflecting improved autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, p62 clearance).  

• Oxidative stress resilience  
  – Under induced oxidative stress (H₂O₂ or blue light), NMN-pretreated RPE should display reduced ROS accumulation (DCFDA assay) and lower apoptotic markers (cleaved caspase-3).  

• Expression of key proteins in RPE  
  – Literature confirms that human RPE express NAMPT, NMNATs 1–3, SIRT1, SIRT3, PGC-1α, TFAM, LC3, and ATG5 (Bhattacharya et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019), supporting the feasibility of the proposed mechanistic readouts.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Mechanistic rationale: Directly targets an age-associated metabolic deficit (declining NAD⁺) implicated in RPE dysfunction.  
  – Broad impact: By boosting sirtuin activity, NMN addresses mitochondrial health, autophagy, oxidative stress, and inflammation—hallmarks of dry AMD pathology.  
  – Safety profile: Early human trials indicate good tolerability, facilitating rapid translation to ocular indications.  
  – Precedent in aging models: Robust preclinical data in multiple tissues suggest efficacy in age-related functional decline.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Ocular bioavailability: Oral NMN’s capacity to reach therapeutic levels in the RPE/choroid is unproven; may require targeted delivery (e.g., intravitreal, periocular, or nanoformulations).  
  – Metabolic fate: Rapid systemic metabolism by CD38 and gut microbiota could limit NMN half-life and tissue uptake.  
  – Off-target effects: Elevating NAD⁺ broadly may affect PARP activity and other NAD⁺-dependent enzymes in unintended ways, potentially impacting cell survival under stress.  
  – Lack of direct AMD data: No published studies have tested NMN in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice), so disease-relevant efficacy remains speculative.  

Conclusion  
Given the established decline of NAD⁺ in aging RPE, the crucial role of SIRT1/SIRT3 in mitochondrial and autophagic homeostasis, and NMN’s favorable safety record, NMN is a compelling candidate for early-stage exploration in dry AMD. The next critical steps are (1) demonstration of RPE/choroidal penetration in vivo, (2) proof-of-concept efficacy in an animal model of dry AMD, and (3) development of an ocular formulation to optimize local delivery and minimize systemic metabolism. If these hurdles are addressed, NMN could become a first-in-class NAD⁺-boosting therapy for dry AMD.

Proposal for Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is a small, water-soluble quinone first identified in bacterial redox enzymes in the 1960s (Hallenbeck et al., 1979). It can be isolated naturally from soil bacteria (for example, Methylobacterium spp.) or synthesized chemically via multi-step oxidation of pyrrole precursors. Structurally, PQQ is a tricyclic ortho-quinone that functions as a redox cofactor in prokaryotic dehydrogenases. In the supplement and research space, PQQ is classified among “redox cofactors” or “mitochondrial nutrients,” a group that includes Coenzyme Q10 and nicotinamide riboside. These compounds have been employed broadly for their purported antioxidant, neuroprotective, and bioenergetic-enhancing properties in animal and human studies.

Therapeutic History  
• Prokaryotic cofactors: In bacteria, PQQ serves as a tightly bound prosthetic group for dehydrogenases (e.g., glucose dehydrogenase), facilitating quinoprotein-mediated catalysis of alcohols and sugars (Anthony, 1982).  
• Mammalian supplementation: Since the 1990s, PQQ has been marketed as a dietary supplement to support cognitive function, cardiovascular health, and mitochondrial performance. Doses in human studies range from 10 to 20 mg/day with no serious adverse events reported up to 20 mg/day for several weeks (Nakano et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2013).  
• Clinical/veterinary uses: Beyond human supplementation, PQQ has shown beneficial effects in rodent models of heart failure, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and metabolic syndrome through mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant pathways (Sakuraba et al., 2014; Chowanadisai et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic precedent: There are no published reports of PQQ tested directly in dry AMD or RPE-specific degeneration models. However, PQQ’s use in models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) underscores its relevance to post-mitotic, energy-dependent cells.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Redox cofactor and ROS signaling  
   – PQQ can cycle between oxidized and reduced forms, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) while at low concentrations promoting mild ROS signaling that activates adaptive stress responses (Rucker et al., 2009).  
2. Activation of mitochondrial biogenesis pathways  
   – PQQ treatment elevates intracellular cAMP and activates CREB phosphorylation, leading to upregulation of PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha), the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis (Chowanadisai et al., 2010).  
   – Downstream, PGC-1α coactivates nuclear respiratory factors (NRF-1/2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), increasing mtDNA replication and expression of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes.  
3. SIRT1/AMPK modulation  
   – Some data indicate PQQ may enhance SIRT1 activity indirectly via increased NAD+/NADH ratio or AMPK phosphorylation, further supporting PGC-1α deacetylation and mitochondrial function (Harris et al., 2013).  
4. Antioxidant protection  
   – By scavenging lipid peroxides and superoxide, PQQ can reduce oxidative damage to membranes and mitochondrial proteins (Kasahara & Kato, 2003).  

Mechanistic relevance to RPE:  
– RPE cells express PGC-1α, NRF-1/2, TFAM, SIRT1, and AMPK, all critical for mitochondrial homeostasis and phagocytic function (Lin et al., 2018).  
– In dry AMD, RPE mitochondrial DNA damage, reduced PGC-1α expression, and impaired oxidative phosphorylation have been documented (Ferrington et al., 2017; Golestaneh et al., 2017), making PQQ’s mechanism directly pertinent.

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay context: Primary human or ARPE-19 cells loaded with fluorescently labeled photoreceptor outer segments (POS), quantifying phagocytosis rate and ATP production.  
– PQQ treatment (1–20 µM) is expected to upregulate PGC-1α and increase mitochondrial mass (as measured by mtDNA copy number and Mitotracker staining) within 24–48 hours (Chowanadisai et al., 2010).  
– Enhanced ETC complex expression and activity (Complex I and IV) should raise basal and maximal respiration (OCR) on Seahorse assays, translating to elevated cellular ATP (Ferrington et al., 2017).  
– The increase in ATP availability and improved oxidative balance should restore energy-dependent processes in RPE, notably the daily phagocytosis of POS. Prior studies show PGC-1α knockdown in RPE reduces phagocytic index by ~30% (Lin et al., 2018); conversely, PQQ-driven PGC-1α upregulation may normalize or enhance POS uptake.  
– Secondary readouts: decreased ROS (DCFDA assay), preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 dye), and reduced markers of cell stress (e.g., CHOP, ATF4).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: PQQ directly targets mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress—two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2017; Golestaneh et al., 2017).  
• Well-characterized safety profile: Human supplementation trials up to 20 mg/day report minimal adverse effects (Nakano et al., 2012).  
• Oral bioavailability: PQQ is orally active, facilitating translational potential.  
• Broad preclinical efficacy: Demonstrated benefits in multiple models of mitochondrial compromise and neurodegeneration.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Retinal penetration unknown: Data on PQQ levels in ocular tissues after systemic dosing are lacking; the blood–retina barrier may limit effective RPE exposure.  
• Dose optimization: Effective in vitro concentrations (micromolar) may not be achievable in vivo without high oral doses or intraocular delivery.  
• Off-target effects: Redox cycling can be a double-edged sword; excessive PQQ may induce pro-oxidant damage in vulnerable cells.  
• Lack of direct AMD models: No published in vivo studies in AMD or RPE degeneration, necessitating proof-of-concept in animal models (e.g., Cfh−/− mice, sodium iodate–induced RPE injury).  

Recommendation  
Proceed to in vitro validation using human RPE cultures challenged with oxidative stress and POS phagocytosis assays. Simultaneously, initiate ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rodents to confirm RPE accumulation. If positive, advance to in vivo dry AMD models for efficacy and safety assessment.

Proposal for CDDO-Im

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Chemical Origins and Class  
   • CDDO-Im (1-[2-cyano-3,12-dioxooleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oyl]imidazole) is a semi-synthetic derivative of the pentacyclic triterpenoid scaffold built on oleanolic acid. It was first described by the Sporn laboratory in the late 1990s as one of a series of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) analogs (Sporn Laboratory, n.d.). Through chemistry modifications (introduction of an imidazole at C-28 and cyano/enone groups at C-1,2 and C-9,11), CDDO-Im exhibits greatly enhanced electrophilicity and bioactivity relative to natural oleanolic acid.  
   • Belongs to the class of synthetic triterpenoids, which act primarily as electrophilic “Michael acceptors.” Other members include CDDO-Me (methyl ester) and CDDO-TFEA. In general, synthetic triterpenoids have been developed as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer agents because of their capacity to modify cysteine sensors on regulatory proteins.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Early Clinical Uses of CDDO Analogs  
   • Anti-inflammatory and anticancer: CDDO-Me advanced into Phase I oncology trials (e.g., lung cancer, lymphoma), demonstrating tolerability at low micromolar plasma concentrations, with on-target activation of Nrf2 biomarkers (NQO1 induction) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (Unknown Reference).  
   • Renal protection: In rodent models of diabetic nephropathy, CDDO analogs attenuated proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis via Nrf2 activation (Unknown Reference).  
   • Ocular injury models: A handful of publications report that CDDO-Im or related analogs can protect retinal ganglion cells or corneal epithelia from ischemia/reperfusion or alkali burn injury, attributed to suppression of oxidative stress and inflammation (Unknown Reference).  

2. Use in Dry AMD or Related Retinal Diseases  
   • There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Im in dry AMD patients.  
   • Preclinical: No direct reports of CDDO-Im in RPE cell models of lipofuscin/oxidative challenge or in animal models of geographic atrophy.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1–Nrf2 Pathway Activation  
   • Electrophilic Michael acceptor groups in CDDO-Im covalently modify reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) in Keap1. This disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 stabilization and nuclear translocation (Dinkova-Kostova et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2013).  
   • Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (AREs) in promoters of genes encoding phase II enzymes (e.g., NQO1, HO-1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), and several detoxification and antioxidant proteins.  

2. Modulation of Autophagy and Lysosomal Biogenesis  
   • Recent studies indicate cross-talk between Nrf2 and TFEB (the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Nrf2 activation can upregulate p62/SQSTM1, which in turn displaces TFEB from lysosomal membranes, promoting nuclear localization of TFEB and transcription of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsins) (Ruiz et al., 2019).  
   • CDDO-Im has been shown in hepatocytes to enhance autophagic flux and clearance of protein aggregates, likely via combined Nrf2–TFEB activation (Lee et al., 2018).  

3. Additional Anti-Inflammatory and Cytoprotective Actions  
   • CDDO-Im inhibits NF-κB signaling by preventing IκB kinase activation, reducing transcription of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) (Liby & Sporn, 2012).  
   • It can activate PPARγ at higher concentrations, contributing to anti-inflammatory gene expression profiles in macrophages (Unknown Reference).  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
1. Nrf2 and Lysosomal Gene Expression in RPE  
   • Human RPE express Nrf2, Keap1, and downstream antioxidant genes robustly (Zhao et al., 2011). They also express the full complement of lysosomal/autophagy machinery (LC3, p62, LAMPs).  
   • In primary or iPSC-derived RPE challenged with photo-oxidative stress or A2E, Nrf2 activation has been shown to decrease ROS and preserve phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Furukawa et al., 2014).  

2. Proposed Assay Readouts  
   • ROS levels (e.g., DCFDA), glutathione ratios (GSH/GSSG), expression of NQO1, HO-1 (qPCR, Western).  
   • Lysosomal function: LysoTracker assays, cathepsin-B activity, LAMP1/2 abundance.  
   • POS clearance: Fluorescently labeled POS uptake and degradation.  
   • Cell viability under oxidative challenge (H2O2, blue-light, A2E).  

3. Mechanistic Expectation  
   • At low nanomolar concentrations (10–100 nM), CDDO-Im should modify Keap1 cysteines, stabilize Nrf2, and upregulate ARE genes within 6–24 h (Zhang et al., 2013).  
   • Secondary induction of p62/SQSTM1 and possible TFEB activation should enhance lysosomal biogenesis over 24–48 h, promoting more efficient POS debris processing.  
   • Net effect: lower intracellular ROS, improved POS clearance, increased RPE survival under chronic stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
   • Potent, well-characterized Nrf2 inducer with proven target engagement in multiple cell types at low nanomolar levels.  
   • Dual action on redox homeostasis and autophagy/lysosomal pathways aligns with core RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (accumulation of lipofuscin, impaired phagocytosis, oxidative injury).  
   • Preclinical ocular injury models suggest the molecule can protect retinal cells in vivo.  
   • Favorable PK in systemic dosing; cell-permeable and stable.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
   • No direct data in dry AMD or RPE-specific disease models—needs orphan disease modeling (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, aged Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice).  
   • Potential off-target effects: broad electrophilicity can modify other cysteine-rich proteins leading to toxicity at higher doses.  
   • Chronic dosing considerations: pro-proliferative or pro-survival signaling could be deleterious if unregulated in the long term.  
   • Ocular delivery route: systemic dosing may not achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina without side effects; local (intravitreal or periocular) formulation and tolerability must be established.  
   • Regulatory precedence: CDDO-Me clinical trials halted for toxicity signals; CDDO-Im clinical experience is limited (Unknown Reference).  

Recommendation  
CDDO-Im represents a rational, mechanism-driven candidate to address oxidative and lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD. Its potent Nrf2 activation and autophagy enhancement make it a strong tool compound for proof-of-concept studies in RPE assays and animal models. Before advancing, we recommend:  
   1. Thorough dose-response and time-course studies in primary human RPE under physiologically relevant stressors (A2E, blue light).  
   2. Assessment of lysosomal function, POS degradation kinetics, and long-term viability.  
   3. In vivo testing in at least one dry AMD animal model to evaluate retinal bioavailability, efficacy, and safety.  
   4. Exploration of ocular-targeted formulations to minimize systemic exposure.  

If these studies confirm on-target activity without undue cytotoxicity, CDDO-Im could be advanced as a lead candidate for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Proposal for Mdivi-1 (Drp1 inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound name: Mitochondrial Division Inhibitor-1 (Mdivi-1)  
• Origin and discovery: Synthetic small molecule first reported in a yeast‐based screen for inhibitors of mitochondrial fission (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008). It was selected for its ability to block dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) GTPase activity and thereby inhibit excessive mitochondrial fragmentation.  
• Chemical class: Non-nucleotide small-molecule inhibitor of dynamin superfamily GTPases. Related compounds have been explored broadly in models of neurodegeneration, cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury and cancer, where modulation of mitochondrial dynamics can influence cell survival.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical uses in non-ocular disease models  
  – Neuroprotective: Mdivi-1 reduced neuronal death after middle cerebral artery occlusion in rats (Qi et al., 2013).  
  – Cardioprotection: Shown to decrease infarct size and preserve cardiac function in rodent ischemia–reperfusion models (Ong et al., 2010).  
  – Cancer models: In vitro, Mdivi-1 impaired mitochondrial fission in various tumor lines, sensitizing cells to chemotherapeutics (Qian et al., 2013).  
• Ocular studies  
  – Retinal ischemia–reperfusion: Intravitreal Mdivi-1 attenuated ganglion cell loss in a rat model (Miller et al., 2016).  
  – Light-induced photoreceptor damage: Mdivi-1 reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in murine bright-light exposure (Wang et al., 2017).  
  – To date, no reported use in dry AMD models or clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary target: Drp1, a cytosolic GTPase that translocates to mitochondria to drive fission.  
  – Mdivi-1 binds Drp1 and inhibits its GTP hydrolysis activity (IC50 ~1–10 μM in biochemical assays).  
  – Prevents Drp1 oligomerization on the mitochondrial outer membrane, shifting balance toward fusion.  
• Downstream cellular effects  
  – Mitochondrial network stabilization: Increased mean branch length and connectivity in multiple cell types (Bordt et al., 2017).  
  – Bioenergetics: Enhanced mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and higher basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) under stress (Qian et al., 2014).  
  – Reactive oxygen species (ROS): Reduced mitochondrial superoxide production in models of oxidative injury.  
• Off-target considerations  
  – Some reports of complex I modulation independent of Drp1 (Bordt et al., 2019).  
  – Concentrations > 50 μM may impair cell viability nonspecifically.  

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Assay  
• RPE expression of Drp1: Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE express DNM1L mRNA and protein (Liu et al., 2015). Drp1 activity increases under oxidative stress, promoting fragmentation.  
• Mechanistic rationale  
  – By preserving mitochondrial network integrity, ATP production for energy-intensive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) should improve.  
  – Lower mitochondrial ROS may reduce cumulative oxidative damage that contributes to RPE senescence in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2013).  
• Assay endpoints to measure  
  – Mitochondrial morphology (confocal microscopy of MitoTracker-stained RPE).  
  – Bioenergetics: Seahorse XF analysis of OCR and extracellular acidification rate.  
  – ROS levels: MitoSOX and general oxidative stress indicators.  
  – Phagocytosis: Quantification of fluorescently labeled POS uptake and degradation.  
  – Viability under chronic H₂O₂ or blue-light stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a key pathomechanism in aging RPE—excessive mitochondrial fission and bioenergetic decline.  
• Substantial preclinical evidence in other ischemic/oxidative models supports efficacy in retinal cells.  
• Orally bioavailable in rodents and penetrates ocular tissues in some studies, facilitating repurposing.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Specificity: Emerging data indicate off-target effects on mitochondrial complex I, raising questions about attributing benefits solely to Drp1 inhibition.  
• Pharmacokinetics/toxicity: Limited published profiles on long-term ocular safety; systemic dosing may lead to unintended effects in non-target tissues.  
• Relevance to dry AMD: Although oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, disease onset is chronic over decades; acute protective effects may not translate to slowing geographic atrophy progression.  
• Drug alternatives: Newer, more selective Drp1 inhibitors (e.g., P110 peptide) or strategies targeting fusion proteins (Mfn2 agonists) may offer improved therapeutic windows.  

Recommendation  
Mdivi-1 represents a mechanistically compelling candidate for in vitro validation in RPE models of dry AMD. Early studies should focus on dose–response in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE under chronic oxidative stress, with robust measures of mitochondrial function and phagocytic capacity. Given concerns about specificity and long-term safety, parallel efforts to assess newer Drp1 modulators or complementary strategies to bolster mitochondrial fusion may be warranted. If in vitro data are favorable, ocular pharmacokinetics, retinal distribution and localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery approaches should be explored before advancing toward in vivo models of geographic atrophy.

Proposal for SRT1720 (SIRT1 activator)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – SRT1720 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. First reported by Milne et al. (2007), it was discovered by high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that enhanced recombinant SIRT1 activity against fluorogenic peptide substrates. Structural optimization around a benzofuran scaffold yielded SRT1720, which exhibits nanomolar potency (EC₅₀ ~0.16 µM in biochemical assays).  
  – Class: Sirtuin‐activating compounds (STACs). These are polyphenol mimetics or heterocyclic small molecules designed to enhance SIRT1 deacetylase activity, promoting downstream deacetylation of PGC-1α, FOXO transcription factors, p53, NF-κB, and other substrates.  

• General uses of STACs  
  – Metabolic disease models (insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)  
  – Lifespan extension and health-span enhancement in worms and rodents  
  – Neuroprotection in models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Metabolic syndrome: In diet‐induced obese mice, oral SRT1720 improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and decreased hepatic steatosis (Feige et al., 2008).  
  – Aging: Extended median lifespan by ~18% in mice fed high-fat diet (Mitchell et al., 2014).  
  – Neurodegeneration: Reportedly reduced β-amyloid burden and improved cognitive performance in transgenic Alzheimer’s models (Kim et al., 2007).  

• Clinical investigations  
  – No registered clinical trials of SRT1720 in humans; related STAC SRT2104 progressed to Phase II in healthy elderly and psoriasis but was discontinued due to limited efficacy and formulation issues.  
  – Safety: Preclinical GLP toxicology indicated acceptable margins; however, clinical data are sparse and limited by poor solubility and formulation.  

• Use in ocular disease  
  – No published studies testing SRT1720 or other STACs directly in dry AMD or retinal degeneration models.  
  – Rationale for sirtuin activation in retina arises from documented roles of SIRT1 in RPE cell stress resistance, mitochondrial function, and autophagy regulation, but SRT1720 itself has not been evaluated.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct molecular targets  
  – Binds an allosteric site on SIRT1 near the N-terminal regulatory domain (residues ~183–230), increasing the enzyme’s Vmax and/or decreasing Km for acetyl-lysine peptide substrates (Hubbard et al., 2013).  
  – Reported to be >100× selective for SIRT1 over SIRT2/3 in vitro, though some studies question strict selectivity.  

• Downstream pathways  
  – Deacetylation and activation of PGC-1α → Upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis genes (NRF1, TFAM)  
  – Deacetylation of FOXO3a → Enhanced transcription of antioxidant enzymes (MnSOD, catalase)  
  – Modulation of autophagy: SIRT1 deacetylates key autophagy proteins (ATG5, ATG7, LC3), promoting autophagosome formation and clearance of damaged mitochondria (Lee et al., 2008).  
  – Crosstalk with AMPK: SIRT1 activation can increase AMPK phosphorylation via LKB1 deacetylation, further promoting mitochondrial homeostasis and autophagy.  

• PK/PD considerations  
  – Oral bioavailability in rodents ~20–30%; half-life ~3–4 h. Tissue distribution includes liver, skeletal muscle; retinal penetration not well characterized.  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assays  
• RPE expression of SIRT1  
  – Human primary and ARPE-19 cells express SIRT1 at both mRNA and protein levels (Gidday et al., 2010). SIRT1 declines with replicative and oxidative stress–induced senescence.  

• Hypothesis‐driven readouts  
  – Mitochondrial biogenesis: Expect upregulation of PGC-1α, increases in mitochondrial DNA copy number, citrate synthase activity.  
  – Autophagy flux: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62/SQSTM1, enhanced co‐localization of LC3 with LAMP1.  
  – POS clearance: In assays feeding ARPE-19 or primary RPE cells isolated bovine POS, SRT1720 should accelerate rhodopsin degradation (e.g., quantified by Western blot) and reduce autofluorescent granule accumulation (lipofuscin proxy).  
  – Oxidative stress resistance: Reduced ROS accumulation under H₂O₂ challenge, increased cell viability, maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 assay).  

• Literature parallels  
  – Resveratrol (a less potent STAC) in RPE reduces oxidative stress and restores autophagy after sodium iodate injury (Han et al., 2015). SRT1720’s superior potency suggests a stronger effect.  
  – In neuronal models, SRT1720 reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence (Calkins et al., 2011), supporting potential to clear age pigments in RPE.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Nanomolar potency and well‐characterized mechanism of direct SIRT1 activation  
  – Established effects on mitochondrial biogenesis, autophagy, and oxidative stress across multiple cell and animal models  
  – Rationale based on documented SIRT1 decline in aging RPE and its central role in pathways disrupted in dry AMD  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Lack of direct preclinical data in RPE or retinal models; no published ocular PK to confirm retinal bioavailability  
  – Potential off-target effects or toxicity at doses required for ocular efficacy; formulation challenges due to poor solubility  
  – Controversies in the field regarding whether STACs directly activate SIRT1 in cells versus acting indirectly via AMPK or other pathways—may complicate mechanistic interpretation  
  – Oral dosing may result in systemic exposure and off‐target SIRT activation in other tissues; topical/ocular delivery may be required but is untested  

Recommendation  
  – Proceed with in vitro validation in human primary RPE and ARPE-19 assays: measure mitochondrial and autophagy markers, POS clearance, lipofuscin accumulation, and cell viability under oxidative stress.  
  – Characterize dose–response and confirm on-target SIRT1 engagement (e.g., acetyl-PGC-1α levels, use of SIRT1 knockdown or selective inhibitor EX-527 as control).  
  – If in vitro data are promising, evaluate ocular PK in rodents and efficacy in RPE‐specific AMD models (e.g., sodium iodate or complement‐mediated injury).  

Conclusion  
SRT1720 is a strong candidate for repurposing in dry AMD assays based on its direct activation of SIRT1, known benefits on mitochondrial and autophagy pathways, and mechanistic alignment with RPE aging phenotypes. Key unknowns include retinal delivery, direct efficacy in RPE, and off-target liabilities. A focused set of in vitro experiments can rapidly de‐risk these aspects and inform go/no-go for preclinical development.
