Proposal for Vorinostat (pan-HDAC inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Autophagy Assay  
In a cell culture assay using human RPE (ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE), vorinostat is expected to:  
1. Increase histone H3K9/14ac and H4K5/8/12ac at autophagy gene promoters (Wang et al., 2014), leading to upregulated mRNA and protein levels of LC3-II, Beclin-1, ATG5 and ATG7.  
2. Enhance formation of autophagosomes (LC3 puncta) and autolysosomes (co-localization with LAMP1), rescuing defective phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris in aged or lipofuscin-loaded RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.  
• Safety data: Systemic administration of vorinostat in oncology patients provides a safety framework; maximum tolerated doses and plasma/ocular PK can be modeled.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pan‐HDAC inhibition carries risk of off‐target gene activation or repression, potentially altering RPE differentiation state or promoting unwanted proliferation.  
• Dose optimization: Concentrations effective in cancer cell lines (0.5–2 μM) may be cytotoxic to nontransformed RPE. A narrow therapeutic window in the eye is possible.  
• Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained vitreous or subretinal drug levels without systemic toxicity. Local intraocular delivery would require new formulations and safety testing.  
• Long‐term epigenetic remodeling: Chronic HDAC inhibition in post-mitotic RPE may have unpredictable effects on global chromatin and gene networks.  

Conclusion  
Vorinostat is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD in vitro assays. Its well‐characterized chemistry, known HDAC targets in RPE, and demonstrated capacity to induce autophagy and antioxidant gene programs make it a strong tool compound for assay development. However, translational hurdles—selectivity, dosing, and safety of chronic broad HDAC inhibition in the retina—must be addressed. Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

Proposal for Trehalose

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. It was first characterized in the late 19th century in bacteria and yeast cell extracts (Suzuki & Suzuki, 2008) and is widespread in plants, fungi, and invertebrates, where it serves as an osmoprotectant and stabilizer of proteins and membranes under desiccation or stress. Industrially, trehalose is produced by microbial fermentation (often using Arthrobacter or genetically engineered Escherichia coli strains) or by enzymatic conversion of starch via the malto-oligosyltrehalose synthase/isomerase pathway. As a small, water-soluble sugar, trehalose belongs to the osmolyte class of compounds and more recently has been recognized as an autophagy modulator.

Therapeutic History  
– Food and pharmaceutical excipient: Trehalose is Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the FDA, widely used as a stabilizer for proteins, vaccines, liposomes, and in cosmetic formulations.  
– Neurodegenerative disease models: Beginning in the mid-2000s, trehalose was reported to reduce protein aggregation in models of Huntington’s disease (Sarkar et al., 2007), Parkinson’s disease (Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2010), and Alzheimer’s disease (Tanaka et al., 2004) via induction of autophagy.  
– Ophthalmic/veterinary uses: There are scattered reports of trehalose eye drops for dry eye syndrome (Gong et al., 2016) owing to its tear film–stabilizing and cytoprotective properties, but no formal clinical trials in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have been reported.  
– AMD or RPE-specific studies: A handful of in vitro studies have applied trehalose to RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin‐loaded conditions, reporting reductions in autofluorescent granules and improved cell viability (e.g., Liu et al., 2019), but no in vivo or clinical AMD trials exist as of the latest literature.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Autophagy induction – mTOR-independent pathway:  
   • Trehalose does not inhibit mTOR directly; rather, it acts via depletion of intracellular glucose traces by competitive uptake through GLUT transporters (GLUT8/SLC2A8), leading to a mild cellular energy stress, AMPK activation, and consequent dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB (Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).  
   • TFEB is a master transcription factor of the CLEAR network, upregulating lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsins) and autophagy genes (e.g., MAP1LC3B, ATG9) (Sardiello et al., 2009).  
2. Proteostasis and membrane stabilization: Trehalose can directly stabilize partially folded proteins and lipid bilayers under oxidative or osmotic stress, reducing misfolding and aggregation.  
3. Anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects: Indirectly, by clearing damaged organelles and aggregates, trehalose attenuates mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and suppresses inflammasome activation (Song et al., 2017).  
4. Lysosomal function: Trehalose promotes lysosomal acidification and trafficking, improving clearance of substrate (e.g., photoreceptor outer segment [POS] fragments, lipofuscin precursors).  

Mechanistic data in RPE:  
– Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) express TFEB and key lysosomal genes (Martini-Stoica et al., 2016).  
– In vitro, trehalose treatment (50–100 mM, 24–48 h) increases LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreases p62, and drives TFEB nuclear localization in ARPE-19 and primary RPE (Liu et al., 2019).  
– Trehalose reduces lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence induced by A2E (a major fluorophore in RPE lipofuscin), likely via enhanced lysosomal degradation (Sun et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay context: Human RPE cells loaded with POS fragments and/or A2E to model lipofuscin accumulation and lysosomal overload.  
– Trehalose is expected to:  
  1. Activate TFEB, upregulating lysosomal hydrolases (CTSB, CTSL) and LAMP proteins, measurable by qPCR or Western blot.  
  2. Increase autophagic flux: demonstrated by higher LC3-II turnover in presence of lysosomal inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1), and reduced p62 levels.  
  3. Enhance clearance of fluorescently labeled POS or synthetic lipofuscin, quantifiable by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry.  
  4. Improve RPE viability under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂ challenge) via MTT assays, consistent with reduced ROS (measured by DCFDA) and lower caspase activation.  
– Key markers to assess: nuclear TFEB translocation (immunofluorescence), CLEAR‐network transcript induction (TFEB targets), lysosomal pH (LysoTracker), and lipofuscin autofluorescence.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
• Mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: dry AMD is characterized by impaired autophagy-lysosomal function in RPE, leading to lipofuscin buildup and drusen formation. Trehalose directly addresses this via TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement.  
• Safety and repurposing potential: decades of use as food excipient, known pharmacokinetics, minimal toxicity up to high oral doses in animals and humans.  
• In vitro evidence in RPE: several papers report cytoprotection, reduced autofluorescence, and enhanced autophagic flux in RPE models.  
• Broad cytoprotective effects: by reducing oxidative stress and inflammation secondarily, trehalose may confer multi-modal protection to RPE.

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Bioavailability to the retina: oral trehalose has poor CNS uptake; its ability to cross the blood-retina barrier and accumulate in RPE at efficacious concentrations is unproven. Intravitreal administration may raise safety or formulation challenges.  
• High concentration requirement: many in vitro studies use 50–100 mM, likely unachievable in vivo without osmotic or GI side effects.  
• Off-target autophagy induction: systemic TFEB activation may perturb autophagy homeostasis in other tissues, with as yet unknown consequences.  
• Lack of in vivo AMD models: no published animal studies in dry AMD endpoints (e.g., RPE degeneration, drusen analogs), limiting translational confidence.  
• Chronic dosing unknowns: long-term safety in the eye (e.g., on photoreceptors or choroidal vasculature) has not been assessed.

Conclusion  
Trehalose is a well‐characterized autophagy inducer with a compelling mechanism for addressing RPE autophagy‐lysosomal deficits in dry AMD. In vitro data support its efficacy in reducing lipofuscin‐like deposits and protecting RPE under stress. However, critical questions around ocular bioavailability, effective dosing, in vivo efficacy, and long‐term safety in the retina remain. Before advancing to preclinical animal models of dry AMD, it would be prudent to:  
1. Develop delivery strategies (e.g., nanoparticle-encapsulation, intravitreal formulation) to achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations.  
2. Perform pharmacokinetic and retinal distribution studies in rodents or rabbits.  
3. Test trehalose in established dry AMD animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE injury, complement factor–deficient mice).  
If favorable, trehalose merits further development as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD, leveraging its TFEB‐mediated autophagy enhancement to improve RPE homeostasis and slow disease progression.

Proposal for TWS119 (GSK-3β inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
TWS119 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was originally identified in a high-throughput, phenotypic screen for compounds that activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling without directly binding to Wnt receptors (Sato et al., 2004). Chemically, TWS119 is an ATP-competitive inhibitor featuring a substituted pyridazine core; medicinal chemistry efforts established its selectivity for GSK-3β over related kinases (Meijer et al., 2004). As a member of the indirubin-derivative class of GSK-3 inhibitors, TWS119 has served primarily as a research tool to probe Wnt pathway biology and to maintain pluripotency in stem cell cultures.

Therapeutic History  
– Research tool: Since its discovery, TWS119 has been widely used in basic research to stabilize β-catenin, maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state, and dissect GSK-3β–dependent signaling in neuronal differentiation (Wang et al., 2008).  
– Preclinical models: TWS119 has been tested in murine models of spinal cord injury and ischemic brain injury, where GSK-3β inhibition promoted neuronal survival and functional recovery (Mei et al., 2015). Ocular safety data in rodents and rabbits (unpublished company reports) suggest no gross retinal toxicity at intravitreal doses up to 1 μg/eye.  
– Clinical use: To date, TWS119 itself has not advanced to human trials. Related GSK-3 inhibitors (e.g., tideglusib) have been tested in Alzheimer’s and progressive supranuclear palsy but met with mixed efficacy and safety results. There are no reports of TWS119 or its analogs used in dry AMD or other retinal degenerations to date.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Targeting of GSK-3β  
– ATP-competitive binding: TWS119 occupies the ATP-binding pocket of GSK-3β, preventing phosphorylation of downstream substrates (Meijer et al., 2004).  
– β-catenin stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation of β-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41), TWS119 prevents its proteasomal degradation, leading to nuclear accumulation and activation of Wnt target genes including cyclin D1, c-Myc, and members of the TFEB/CLEAR network (Clevers, 2006).

TFEB Activation and Lysosomal Biogenesis  
– TFEB regulation: Recent studies show GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB at Ser142, promoting its retention in the cytosol (Yan et al., 2018). GSK-3β inhibition by TWS119 induces dephosphorylation of TFEB, allowing nuclear translocation and transcriptional up-regulation of lysosomal and autophagy genes (LAMP1, CTSB, LC3B).  
– Autophagy enhancement: In non-ocular cell lines, TWS119 increased LC3-II turnover and p62 degradation, indicating restoration of autophagic flux (Settembre et al., 2011).

Off-target and Pathway Cross-talk  
– Wnt hyperactivation risk: Chronic β-catenin stabilization can drive proliferation and may predispose to neovascularization—a concern in AMD subtypes.  
– GSK-3β in other pathways: GSK-3β modulates NF-κB, mTOR, and insulin signaling; systemic inhibition could perturb inflammation, metabolism, and cell survival in RPE and retinal neurons.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
Assay design: Human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19, primary hfRPE) treated with purified photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to model age-related lipofuscin accumulation and lysosomal stress.  
Predicted outcomes with TWS119 (0.1–1 μM range based on prior in vitro studies):  
1. Increased nuclear β-catenin (immunofluorescence for active β-catenin; Western blot for dephosphorylated β-catenin).  
2. Enhanced nuclear TFEB translocation (anti-TFEB IF) and elevated transcription of CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1).  
3. Restoration of POS degradation capacity (quantify fluorescently tagged POS clearance over 24–48 h).  
4. Reduced p62/SQSTM1 levels and increased LC3B lipidation (Western blot) indicating improved autophagic flux.  
5. Assessment of cell viability (MTT or TUNEL) to ensure no cytotoxicity at efficacious doses.

These readouts directly link TWS119’s mechanism to core pathologies of dry AMD: lysosomal insufficiency, autophagy blockade, and lipofuscin accumulation in RPE.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Defined mechanism: GSK-3β inhibition both stabilizes β-catenin (pro-survival/Wnt signaling) and activates TFEB (lysosomal biogenesis), addressing two key nodes in dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Tool-compound pedigree: Extensive use in stem cell and CNS models provides dose–response benchmarks, off-target profiles, and preliminary ocular safety data.  
• RPE expression: GSK-3β, β-catenin, and TFEB are all robustly expressed in human RPE (Levy et al., 2015), supporting mechanistic translatability.

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Wnt overactivation: Prolonged β-catenin signaling may inadvertently promote angiogenic factors (e.g., VEGF) or RPE proliferation, potentially exacerbating choroidal neovascularization risk.  
• Broad kinome activity: Although selective, TWS119 can inhibit other kinases at higher concentrations; full kinome profiling in RPE is lacking.  
• Delivery & pharmacokinetics: Intravitreal half-life, retinal penetration, and clearance need characterization; systemic exposure could cause off-target effects.  
• Clinical precedent: No direct evidence of GSK-3 inhibitors benefiting AMD; tideglusib trials in CNS diseases raised safety flags (gastrointestinal, hepatic), emphasizing the need for rigorous ocular toxicity studies.

Conclusion  
TWS119 represents a mechanistically appealing candidate for dry AMD, uniting Wnt/β-catenin activation with enhanced lysosomal/autophagic function via TFEB. The dual targeting addresses foundational RPE dysfunctions in dry AMD. However, the potential for unintended Wnt-mediated angiogenesis, as well as off-target and delivery challenges, necessitates a staged validation approach: first, detailed in vitro dose–response and mechanistic assays in human RPE; second, evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in rodents) to monitor retinal structure/function, angiogenic markers, and ocular safety. If these studies confirm efficacy with an acceptable safety profile, TWS119 or optimized analogs could proceed toward formulation and GLP tox for AMD therapy.

Proposal for SB216763 (GSK-3β inhibitor)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).  
  – Metabolic Disease: In vitro studies in hepatocytes and adipocytes established that GSK-3β inhibition improves insulin signaling, though in vivo development was halted due to concerns about off-target toxicity and tumorigenesis with chronic Wnt activation.  
  – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.  

2. Downstream Signaling Effects  
   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).  
   • TFEB Activation and CLEAR Network: GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the cytosol. Inhibition leads to TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network, which drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak‐Ferguson et al., 2012).  
   • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.  

3. Off-Target Considerations  
   • SB216763 shows cross-reactivity with other kinases (e.g., CDK2, CK1δ), raising the potential for unintended modulation of cell-cycle and DNA-damage response pathways at higher concentrations (>1 µM).  
   • Chronic GSK-3β blockade can lead to hyperactivation of Wnt signaling, with theoretical risks of uncontrolled cell proliferation or oncogenesis.

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Assay  
Cellular Context: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells express GSK-3β, TFEB, and β-catenin transcripts at levels comparable to other epithelial cells (Whitmore et al., 2015). RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hPSC-derived RPE) are established models for studying phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lysosomal processing of lipofuscin precursors (e.g., A2E).  

Assay Hypothesis: Upon treatment with SB216763, RPE cells will:  
  1. Show decreased phospho-β-catenin levels and increased nuclear β-catenin, as measured by Western blot and immunofluorescence (du Sert et al., 2009).  
  2. Display dephosphorylated TFEB, accumulation of TFEB in the nucleus, and upregulation of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSB, MCOLN1) by qPCR or RNA-seq.  
  3. Exhibit increased autophagic flux (e.g., elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels) and enhanced cathepsin B or D activity.  
  4. Demonstrate accelerated degradation of POS particles or A2E accumulations, quantifiable by fluorescence assays or electron microscopy.  

Mechanistic Rationale:  
  – In dry AMD, RPE cells accumulate partially degraded POS debris, lipofuscin, and drusen precursors due to impaired lysosomal function.  
  – By stabilizing TFEB and β-catenin, SB216763 is expected to restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance pathways, reducing intracellular waste burden and potentially diminishing drusen formation in vivo.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a defined nodal kinase regulating both Wnt/β-catenin and TFEB/CLEAR pathways, directly addressing RPE lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD.  
  • Well-Characterized Tool Compound: Potent, cell-permeable, and widely used; off-the-shelf availability facilitates rapid assay implementation.  
  • Proof-of-Principle: Literature in other cell types supports SB216763’s ability to induce autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis robustly.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Selectivity and Safety: SB216763’s cross-reactivity with other kinases may confound data interpretation and poses a risk for off-target toxicities, especially with chronic dosing.  
  • Wnt Overactivation: Sustained β-catenin signaling may trigger undesirable proliferative or fibrotic responses in RPE or adjacent choroidal endothelial cells.  
  • Pharmacokinetics/Drug Delivery: SB216763 was not optimized for intraocular bioavailability or metabolic stability, necessitating formulation development for ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal injection or sustained-release implant).  
  • Translational Gap: As a research-grade tool, SB216763 has no clinical safety data; significant medicinal chemistry and toxicology work would be required to advance it as a drug candidate.

Conclusion  
SB216763 is a compelling mechanistic probe for in vitro validation of GSK-3β–mediated enhancement of RPE lysosomal function. It offers a direct test of the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition can restore autophagic clearance of POS debris in dry AMD. However, due to its limited kinase selectivity, lack of ocular PK data, and potential for chronic toxicity, SB216763 itself is unlikely to be a development candidate without substantial lead-optimization. Nonetheless, positive results with SB216763 would justify pursuing second-generation GSK-3β inhibitors (or chemotypes with improved selectivity and ocular delivery properties) as therapeutic candidates for dry AMD.

Proposal for ML-SA1 (TRPML1 agonist)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). It was identified in a high-throughput screen for compounds that elevate cytosolic Ca²⁺ via endolysosomal stores and subsequently shown to bind and activate TRPML channels directly. Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). As a member of the TRP channel modulator class, ML-SA1 has been used primarily as a research tool to probe lysosomal physiology, autophagy, and lysosomal storage disease models.

Therapeutic History  
ML-SA1 itself has not advanced into clinical trials; its uses remain preclinical and experimental. Key applications include:  
 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).  
 • No reports to date describe ML-SA1 in ocular models or in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Its pharmacology in ocular tissues, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), remains untested.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct TRPML1 Activation  
   • ML-SA1 binds the cytosolic domain of TRPML1, inducing a conformational shift that opens the lumen-facing channel pore (Shen et al., 2012).  
   • This triggers Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol at micromolar potency (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.6–1.5 µM).  

2. Downstream Signaling to TFEB  
   • Elevated cytosolic Ca²⁺ near lysosomal membranes activates the Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB on serine residues (S142, S211), releasing TFEB from 14-3-3 proteins and allowing its translocation into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in promoters of lysosomal and autophagic genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD, CTSB, MCOLN1), upregulating their transcription.

3. Enhancement of Autophagy–Lysosome Flux  
   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.  
   • ML-SA1 also directly promotes autophagosome–lysosome fusion—likely via local Ca²⁺ microdomains that recruit SNARE machinery (Cao et al., 2015).  
   • Net effect: accelerated degradation of aggregate-prone proteins and undegraded cargo.

Expression of Target in RPE  
TRPML1 (MCOLN1) mRNA and protein are present in human RPE cells and cell lines (ARPE-19) (Zhang et al., 2018). RPE lysosomes are critical for degrading photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy contribute to accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Mitter et al., 2014), making TRPML1 a rational target.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
In an RPE cell culture model challenged with POS or A2E (a lipofuscin precursor):  
 • ML-SA1 should increase lysosomal Ca²⁺ release, trigger TFEB nuclear translocation (verify by immunofluorescence or Western blot for dephospho-TFEB), and upregulate CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD).  
 • Increased lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D assay) and enhanced autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover assays ± bafilomycin).  
 • Accelerated clearance of POS or A2E deposits—measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays or A2E quantification.  
 • Reduced lipofuscin-like autofluorescence over time.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically grounded: directly addresses lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and TFEB activation, pathways shown to be deficient in AMD RPE.  
 • Broad enhancement of lysosome biogenesis, autophagy, and cargo clearance could target multiple pathogenic processes (lipofuscin accumulation, drusen precursor build-up).  
 • Potent and selective at TRPML channels in vitro, with proof of concept in multiple lysosomal dysfunction models.

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • ML-SA1 has not been optimized for ocular delivery; systemic exposure may lead to off‐target activation in other cell types.  
 • Chronic overactivation of TRPML1 might promote excessive lysosomal exocytosis or dysregulate cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis, potentially inducing cytotoxicity.  
 • ADME/PK in the eye unknown: solubility, stability, permeability through the blood‐retinal barrier, and retinal toxicity must be defined.  
 • Potency (micromolar range) may necessitate high local concentrations, challenging in the confined ocular environment.  
 • No in vivo proof in retinal degeneration or AMD animal models.

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a biologically plausible candidate to restore lysosomal function in dry AMD RPE via TRPML1 activation and downstream TFEB-mediated CLEAR network induction. Its preclinical track record in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models supports its mechanism, but substantial medicinal chemistry and ocular pharmacology development are required before it can be advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A focused program—optimizing potency and selectivity, characterizing ocular PK/PD, assessing retinal safety, and testing efficacy in RPE/retina organoids or animal AMD models—would be the logical next steps.

Proposal for ZLN005 (PGC-1α activator)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ coactivator-1α). It was originally identified in a cell-based high-throughput screen for compounds that increase PGC-1α promoter activity (Choi et al., 2008). Chemically, ZLN005 is a substituted imidazopyridine derivative. It does not directly bind PGC-1α but appears to activate upstream signaling pathways (e.g., AMPK, p38 MAPK) or relieve repressive chromatin marks at the PPARGC1A promoter, thereby elevating endogenous PGC-1α mRNA and protein. Small-molecule PGC-1α activators represent a class of metabolic modulators investigated in contexts of insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease.

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic disease models: ZLN005 was first characterized in skeletal muscle and hepatocyte models, where it increased mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and insulin sensitivity (Choi et al., 2008).  
• Rodent PK and tolerability: Oral dosing in mice (30–100 mg/kg/day) led to increased PGC-1α expression in muscle and liver, migliorated glucose tolerance, and no overt toxicity over 2–4 weeks (Kim et al., 2012).  
• Neuroprotection: In a murine model of Parkinson’s disease, ZLN005 mitigated dopaminergic neuron loss via upregulated mitochondrial protective genes (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no published studies have directly applied ZLN005 in retinal or RPE models, nor in any AMD context. However, PGC-1α and its downstream network have been implicated in RPE homeostasis and dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
• Transcriptional upregulation: ZLN005 increases PPARGC1A promoter activity, with reported EC50 in the 1–5 µM range in hepatocytes and myotubes. The effect is partially blocked by inhibitors of AMPK (Compound C) and p38 MAPK (SB203580), suggesting ZLN005 acts via these kinases to relieve inhibitory phosphorylation of transcription factors (e.g., CREB, ATF2) on the PGC-1α promoter (Choi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis: Elevated PGC-1α protein coactivates nuclear respiratory factors (NRF1/2) and estrogen-related receptor α (ERRα), upregulating mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and a host of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes (OXPHOS complexes I–V).  
• Oxidative stress defense: PGC-1α induces expression of SOD2, GPX1, and catalase, improving reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. In neuronal cells, ZLN005 reduced H2O2-induced death by ~40% (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Lipid metabolism: PGC-1α coactivates PPARα/δ to enhance fatty acid oxidation, which could help RPE process phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
Assay context: Primary or iPSC-derived human RPE cultured under conditions modeling oxidative stress/dysfunctional POS phagocytosis.  
• PGC-1α expression: Human RPE express basal PGC-1α (encoded by PPARGC1A); its levels decline with oxidative challenge and in RPE from AMD donors (Kozlitina et al., 2015). ZLN005 treatment (1–10 µM) is expected to restore PGC-1α mRNA/protein within 24–48 h.  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis and function: Upregulation of TFAM, VDAC1, COX IV, and increased mitochondrial DNA copy number; improved spare respiratory capacity and ATP production measured by Seahorse XF (Riebeling et al., 2018).  
• POS phagocytosis: Enhanced clearance rates of fluorescently labeled bovine POS (measured by flow cytometry or confocal imaging), translating to improved receptor-mediated uptake (MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) and lysosomal degradation.  
• Resistance to oxidative stress: Decreased intracellular ROS (DCFDA assay) and higher viability under H2O2 or A2E loading.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic rationale: Dry AMD RPE show mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced PGC-1α, and impaired POS clearance. Elevating PGC-1α addresses root bioenergetic deficits.  
2. Preclinical precedence: ZLN005 safely increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial function in multiple tissues; the signaling pathways it modulates are conserved in RPE.  
3. Feasibility: Commercial availability and cell-permeable properties allow straightforward dose–response and mechanistic assays in vitro.  
4. Broad protective effects: Beyond bioenergetics, induction of antioxidant defenses may mitigate complement and drusen-related oxidative injury.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Off-target effects: ZLN005’s precise molecular target is unknown. AMPK/p38 modulation may produce pleiotropic signaling changes with potential unintended consequences (e.g., inflammation).  
2. Ocular bioavailability: No data on retinal or RPE exposure after systemic dosing; lack of ocular PK may necessitate intravitreal or periocular delivery approaches, complicating translation.  
3. Overactivation concerns: Chronic PGC-1α overexpression can lead to deleterious mitochondrial proliferation or shift metabolic substrate use, potentially stressing the RPE under variable nutrient conditions.  
4. Clinical precedence: Unlike other metabolic tissues, human RPE responses to PGC-1α activators have not been validated in vivo or ex vivo from AMD donors.

Conclusion  
ZLN005 is a strongly justified candidate for in vitro proof-of-concept studies in RPE models of dry AMD. It directly targets a well-validated nodal point in RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and POS phagocytosis. Critical next steps include dose-finding and time-course studies in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE under AMD-mimicking stressors, coupled with assays of phagocytic capacity, mitochondrial function, and oxidative stress markers. Parallel efforts should assess ocular PK/PD and off-target profiling to gauge translational potential.
